research.notes: WAVE-2 SYNTHESIS — what the new engines change for the RTX 5090 / Win11 rig: 1) mistral.rs is the standout wave-2 add: it is the only NEW engine here that is Windows-NATIVE, single-binary, AND Blackwell-capable today. It slots between Ollama (easiest) and vLLM (highest throughput) — a Rust-native OpenAI server with PagedAttention + FP8 KV-cache quant + ISQ (quantize any HF model in-situ, no pre-conversion) + FA2/3 + speculative decoding. For a local LLM-crew studio it covers single-user serving without WSL2, and ISQ means you can run a fresh HF model the day it drops without waiting for a GGUF. Status: runner-up to llama.cpp for the daily driver because the GGUF ecosystem is still deeper. 2) Triton Inference Server changes NOTHING for this rig directly — Windows support was DEPRECATED at 25.01 / v2.51.0 and there is NO Windows release after that. It is now Linux/Docker-only and folded into NVIDIA Dynamo. It is Blackwell-capable (26.02+ lists Blackwell) but only matters here as the eventual production-serving layer in front of TRT-LLM/vLLM if the studio ever ships a Linux box or cloud endpoint. Catalogued as situational/reference, not a daily-driver on this machine. 3) MLX + mlx-lm is pure cross-platform REFERENCE — Apple-Silicon-only, will not run on the RTX 5090 at all. Useful only because the studio's published recipes/docs may target Mac readers; do not install it here. THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT CONFIG TAKEAWAY for this lane on this rig: on Blackwell sm_120, the CUDA TOOLKIT VERSION is the dominant performance lever, not the engine choice. Build/run llama.cpp (and source-built vLLM) against CUDA 12.8 with CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 and GGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS=OFF so the Blackwell MMQ kernels engage — that is ~6x faster prefill (5611 pp / 211 tg vs 989 pp / 146 tg on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) than the cuBLAS fallback. CUDA 13.x currently CRASHES the Blackwell MMQ kernel (segfault) and silently falls back to cuBLAS, so a "13.1 prebuilt" is a 5x-slower trap. Pin CUDA 12.8 across the whole lane (llama.cpp, vLLM source build, torch cu128 for Unsloth) and you get the rig's full throughput; mismatch the toolkit and you lose most of the 5090.

extras.name: llamacpp-blackwell-cuda128-source-build-and-serve
extras.note: THE load-bearing build for this rig. Use CUDA 12.8 (NOT 13.x — 13.x crashes the Blackwell MMQ kernel and silently falls back to ~5x-slower cuBLAS). Linux/WSL2: `export PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.8/bin:$PATH; rm -rf build; cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS=OFF -DCUDAToolkit_ROOT=/usr/local/cuda-12.8; cmake --build build --config Release -j $(nproc)`. Windows native: install VS2022 C++ workload + CUDA Toolkit 12.8, then `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS=OFF; cmake --build build --config Release`. ALWAYS delete build/ before reconfiguring (stale cache keeps FORCE_CUBLAS=ON). Verified Blackwell numbers (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B): CUDA12.8+MMQ pp512=5611-6566 t/s, tg128=201-211 t/s vs cuBLAS pp=989 tg=146 — ~6x prefill / 1.4x decode. Serve a dense 32B Q4_K_M fully on the 5090's 32GB: `llama-server -m model-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080`. (Caveat: if you hit 'CUDA error: invalid resource handle' on a specific model's custom kernel, that build's MXFP4/MMQ path is unstable — fall back to a CUDA-12 prebuilt or an earlier commit.)

extras.name: llamacpp-windows-prebuilt-cuda12-fast-path
extras.note: No-compile Windows path (build b9484, 2026-06-02). The official Releases page ships BOTH 'Windows x64 (CUDA 12)' and 'Windows x64 (CUDA 13)' zips plus separate cudart DLL packs (CUDA 12.4 DLLs / CUDA 13.3 DLLs, ~373MB each). For Blackwell PICK THE CUDA 12 BUILD, not CUDA 13 (13.x = MMQ-kernel crash -> cuBLAS fallback -> ~5x slower). Steps: download `llama-bXXXX-bin-win-cuda-12.4-x64.zip` + the matching `cudart-llama-bin-win-cuda-12.4-x64.zip`, unzip both into the same folder, drop your.gguf in, run `llama-server.exe -m model.gguf -ngl 99 -c 32768 -fa`. This is the fastest way to get a Blackwell-correct llama.cpp on Windows without VS2022/CMake; only switch to the source build (recipe above) if you need a bleeding-edge commit or a custom flag.

extras.name: llamacpp-moe-cpu-offload-64gb-ram-n-cpu-moe
extras.note: Run a big MoE (e.g. Qwen3.5-235B-A22B or gpt-oss-120B class) that won't fit in 32GB VRAM by keeping attention/dense tensors on the 5090 and offloading expert FFN tensors to the 64GB system RAM. `llama-server -m moe-model-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 24 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 --threads 16` — `--n-cpu-moe N` moves N layers' worth of MoE experts to CPU; raise N until it fits VRAM, lower it for speed. This is the single biggest reason the 64GB RAM matters on this rig: it turns 'too big for 32GB' into 'runs at usable tok/s'. Pair with the CUDA-12.8 MMQ build above so the on-GPU portion stays fast. For dense models that DO fit, skip --n-cpu-moe entirely and use -ngl 99.

extras.name: mistralrs-windows-cuda-cargo-build-and-isq-serve
extras.note: Native-Windows OpenAI server, no WSL2 (v0.8.3). Prereq: Rust toolchain + CUDA Toolkit 12.8 + (optional) cuDNN. Build the server with CUDA + FlashAttention: `cargo install --git https://github.com/EricLBuehler/mistral.rs.git --features "cuda flash-attn cudnn" mistralrs-server`. Serve a plain HF model with ISQ (in-situ quant — no GGUF needed): `mistralrs-server --isq Q4K -i plain -m Qwen/Qwen3-14B` for interactive, or as an OpenAI endpoint on :1234: `mistralrs-server --port 1234 plain -m Qwen/Qwen3-14B --isq Q4K`. PagedAttention is ON by default on CUDA; halve KV memory with FP8 KV cache via `--pa-cache-type f8e4m3`. To serve an existing GGUF instead: `mistralrs-server --port 1234 gguf -m./ -f model-Q4_K_M.gguf`. Use `--no-paged-attn` only if you hit a kernel issue. This is the recommended daily Windows server when you want to run a model the day it lands on HF without waiting for a GGUF conversion.

extras.name: vllm-wsl2-ubuntu-source-build-sm120-cu128
extras.note: vLLM on Blackwell = build from source in WSL2 (prebuilt PyPI wheels throw 'no kernel image is available'/'sm_120 not compatible'). In WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 with CUDA 12.8 toolkit: `uv venv --python 3.12 --seed && source.venv/bin/activate`; `pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128`; `git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm && cd vllm && python use_existing_torch.py && pip install -r requirements/build.txt`; then `export TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST="12.0"; export VLLM_FLASH_ATTN_VERSION=2; MAX_JOBS=6 pip install --no-build-isolation -e.` (TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0 is mandatory so kernels compile for sm_120). Serve a 32B AWQ within 32GB VRAM: `vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-32B-AWQ --quantization awq_marlin --max-model-len 16384 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --kv-cache-dtype fp8`. Drop --max-model-len / raise quant if you OOM. Alternative no-build route: vLLM also publishes cu128 and cu130 binary variants (default is cu129) — try `pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/cu128` before committing to a 30-min source build.

extras.name: vllm-native-windows-prebuilt-wheel-py313-blackwell
extras.note: Experimental but real: native-Windows vLLM 0.21.0 for Blackwell sm_120 with NO WSL2/Docker. Create a Python 3.13 venv, then: `pip install torch==2.11.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128`; `pip install triton-windows==3.6.0.post26`; `pip install vllm-0.21.0+cu128-cp313-cp313-win_amd64.whl` (from the repo's release assets); `pip install "llguidance>=1.3.0,<1.4.0" "xgrammar>=0.2.0,<1.0.0"`; `pip install git+https://github.com/aivrar/multi-turboquant.git`. The build fixes the Windows-specific bugs that previously blocked `vllm serve`, and adds 10 KV-cache compression dtypes (up to 2x KV capacity vs FP16) — launch with e.g. `vllm serve <model> --kv-cache-dtype turboquant_k8v4 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9`. Caveat: kernels are cuobjdump-verified but full RTX 50-series runtime confirmation is still community-pending — treat as a convenience path, keep the WSL2 source build as the trusted fallback.

extras.name: unsloth-blackwell-qlora-14b-in-32gb-vram
extras.note: QLoRA a 14B in the 5090's 32GB. INSTALL is the gotcha on Blackwell: standard PyPI unsloth lacks Blackwell hybrid-attention kernels. Best path on Windows: install Unsloth Studio (`curl -fsSL unsloth.ai/install.sh | sh`) which provisions a Python-3.13 venv with Blackwell-tuned kernels. Lighter path: `uv pip install unsloth --torch-backend=auto` (auto-selects cu128) into a venv that already has torch cu128. CONFIG (validated shape on RTX 5090 32GB): `from unsloth import FastLanguageModel; model, tok = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(model_name='unsloth/Qwen3-14B', max_seq_length=4096, load_in_4bit=True, dtype=None)`; then `model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=32, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0, target_modules=['q_proj','k_proj','v_proj','o_proj','gate_proj','up_proj','down_proj'], use_gradient_checkpointing='unsloth', random_state=3407)`. TrainingArguments: `per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, learning_rate=2e-4, optim='paged_adamw_8bit', bf16=True, warmup_steps=10, lora rank 32 on all linear layers`. The paged_adamw_8bit optimizer pages optimizer state to the 64GB system RAM under VRAM pressure — that plus 4-bit base is what keeps a 14B (and even a 30B-class with seq<=2048) inside 32GB. Bump max_seq_length down / batch to 1 if you OOM.

extras.name: ollama-blackwell-windows-flags-and-context
extras.note: Easiest daily driver on this rig (Ollama bundles a Blackwell-correct CUDA llama.cpp — no build). Windows: install the Ollama app, then tune via env vars (System > Environment): `OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1` (enable FA), `OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0` (halve KV memory at near-lossless quality), `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=2` and `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=2` for the LLM-crew serving the studio. Pull + run a 32B that fits 32GB: `ollama run qwen3:32b`; force full GPU offload and a 32K window with a Modelfile: `FROM qwen3:32b` + `PARAMETER num_gpu 99` + `PARAMETER num_ctx 32768`, then `ollama create qwen3-32k -f Modelfile`. Note: the MLX backend in the Ollama blog is Apple-Silicon-only and does NOT apply here — on the 5090 Ollama uses its CUDA backend. Use Ollama for convenience/agents; reach for the CUDA-12.8 llama.cpp source build when you need the last 20% of throughput or --n-cpu-moe.

research.notes: Wave-2 lane synthesis. The new engines reshape the local serving picture for this single 5090/Windows rig in three ways. (1) The Windows-native floor is now genuinely solid: Ollama v0.30 lists the RTX 5090 (sm_120) as fully supported, ships its own CUDA 12.8 runtime, and serves OpenAI-compatible on :11434 with zero build steps — it is the correct default for local-LLM delegation, ComfyUI-adjacent agents, and "just give me a model" workloads. (2) For maximum single-GPU INT4 throughput, the EXL3/ExLlamaV3 stack via TabbyAPI is the throughput king on consumer NVIDIA — its `start.bat` auto-detects CUDA and builds the right ExLlamaV3 wheel on Windows natively, no WSL2, and EXL3 (QTIP-derived) holds lower perplexity than GGUF/AWQ at equal bitrate while quantized KV cache (Q4/Q6) frees context room. (3) Routing/multi-model is now built into llama.cpp itself: llama-server Router Mode (shipped 2025-12-11) gives `--models-dir` + `--models-max` + LRU eviction + `/models/load|unload` in-process, making the external llama-swap proxy optional for many setups — one server, many GGUFs, dynamic swap, all native Windows. The heavier vLLM/Aphrodite path remains WSL2-only on this rig (their compiled sm_120 kernels expect cu128 while the PyPI resolver pulls cu130 torch — a real, current landmine), and GPUStack v2 dropped native-Windows workers entirely (WSL2 only now), so the datacenter-style orchestration tier costs you a Linux userland. THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT CONFIG TAKEAWAY: never run an engine on this 5090 in eager mode. Across vLLM on WSL2 the same Qwen3-14B-AWQ measured ~17 tok/s with --enforce-eager vs ~140 tok/s with CUDA graphs enabled (8x) — CUDA graphs / FlashInfer are not optional on Blackwell. The equivalent levers everywhere else: Ollama set OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1 + OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0; llama.cpp build with -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 and launch with -fa --cache-type-k q8_0; TabbyAPI keep cache_mode at Q6/Q8 and never fall back to FP16 KV unless you have headroom. Quantize the KV cache, keep CUDA graphs on, and pin sm_120 at build time — that trio is what turns 32 GB into a 32B-class serving box.

engines.summary: llama.cpp's built-in answer to llama-swap: a router that exposes /models, /models/load, /models/unload and forwards each request to the right model instance based on the OpenAI `model` field — no external proxy process. Point it at a folder with --models-dir (or let it auto-discover from LLAMA_CACHE), cap concurrent residents with --models-max (default 4, LRU eviction), or require explicit loads with --no-models-autoload. Per-model overrides live in a --models-preset config.ini (ctx-size, temp, etc.); global flags after the binary apply to every model. Because it is the same llama-server binary, it gets the full Blackwell story for free — build with -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120, run with -fa and quantized KV (--cache-type-k q8_0), and you have a native-Windows multi-model router with CPU/RAM MoE offload (--n-cpu-moe) usable on the 64 GB system RAM. This is the in-lane alternative to the wave-1 llama-swap proxy and to a degree to Ollama's model management, with zero added moving parts.

extras.name: ollama-blackwell-windows-native-tuned-serve
extras.note: Ollama v0.30 on native Windows 11, RTX 5090 (sm_120), no Toolkit needed (bundles CUDA 12.8). Install the Windows.exe from ollama.com, then set tuning env vars in an elevated PowerShell so the service picks them up: [System.Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION','1','Machine'); [System.Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE','q8_0','Machine'); [System.Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL','4','Machine'); [System.Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS','3','Machine'); [System.Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE','30m','Machine') then restart the Ollama tray app. q8_0 KV halves cache memory at near-zero quality loss and REQUIRES flash attention on. Pull and run a 32B-class model that fits 32 GB at Q4: ollama pull qwen2.5:32b-instruct-q4_K_M; ollama run qwen2.5:32b-instruct-q4_K_M. OpenAI-compatible smoke test: curl http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"qwen2.5:32b-instruct-q4_K_M","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}'. Expect ~48 tok/s on the 32B Q4; ~140 tok/s on an 8B Q4. If nvidia-smi shows the model on CPU / '0 B VRAM' (issue #13338), update the NVIDIA driver and confirm OLLAMA_LLM_LIBRARY isn't forced to cpu.

extras.name: llamacpp-blackwell-cuda128-build-and-server
extras.note: Build llama.cpp for Blackwell sm_120 on Windows (Visual Studio 2022 + CUDA Toolkit 12.8 installed). From a 'x64 Native Tools' prompt in the repo: cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DLLAMA_CURL=ON then cmake --build build --config Release -j. Single dense model, full offload, flash attention + q8_0 KV: build\bin\Release\llama-server.exe -m models\Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080. MoE partial CPU offload to exploit the 64 GB system RAM (keep attention on GPU, push expert FFN to CPU) — e.g. a large MoE that won't fully fit: llama-server.exe -m models\BigMoE-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 24 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0. --n-cpu-moe N offloads N layers' expert tensors to RAM; raise N until it fits VRAM, lower for speed. sm_120 build MUST set CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 or you get fallback/JIT and slow first run.

extras.name: llamacpp-router-mode-multimodel-windows
extras.note: llama.cpp Router Mode (shipped 2025-12-11) = native-Windows multi-model router, no llama-swap proxy. Same Blackwell build as above. Point at a GGUF folder, cap residents, apply global flags to every model: build\bin\Release\llama-server.exe --models-dir E:\AI-Models\gguf --models-max 2 -ngl 99 -c 16384 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080. --models-max 2 keeps at most two models in 32 GB VRAM and LRU-evicts the third on demand. Route by the OpenAI model field — no client change beyond the name: curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -d '{"model":"Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'. List/status: curl http://localhost:8080/models (states: loaded|loading|unloaded). Manual control: POST /models/load and /models/unload with {"model":"<file>.gguf"}. Per-model context/sampler presets via --models-preset config.ini ([model-name] then ctx-size=, temp=). Use --no-models-autoload to force explicit loads. This is the in-lane replacement for the wave-1 llama-swap front for most single-rig setups.

extras.name: tabbyapi-exl3-5090-windows-native-int4-throughput
extras.note: TabbyAPI native Windows (no WSL2) for max single-GPU INT4 throughput via EXL3. git clone https://github.com/theroyallab/tabbyAPI; cd tabbyAPI; then run.\start.bat — it auto-detects CUDA 12.8 and installs matching ExLlamaV3 + FlashAttention wheels (pick the cu128/Blackwell option if prompted). Edit config.yml for the 32 GB 5090: model: model_dir: models/Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct-exl3-4.0bpw; backend: exllamav3; max_seq_len: 32768; cache_size: 32768; cache_mode: "6,6" (ExLlamaV3 takes k_bits,v_bits 2-8; 6,6 ≈ Q6 KV, drop to "4,4" for more context room); chunk_size: 2048; tensor_parallel: false; gpu_split_auto: true. Speculative decoding for 1.5-2x: draft_model_name: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-exl3 + draft_model_dir + draft_cache_mode: "6,6". network: host 0.0.0.0, port 5000. Launch:.\start.bat; OpenAI endpoint at http://localhost:5000/v1, FastAPI docs at /docs. EXL3 holds lower perplexity than AWQ/GGUF at equal bitrate; on 24 GB the EXL2 70B 4.0bpw + Q4 KV path hit ~22 tok/s where AWQ vLLM OOM'd — the 32 GB 5090 has headroom for ~4.5bpw + Q6. NOTE: AGPL-3.0, self-described 'hobby project not for production servers' — fine for this single-user rig, review before product use.

extras.name: vllm-wsl2-5090-cuda-graphs-awq-32b-serve
extras.note: vLLM on the 5090 is WSL2-only and the #1 trap is the torch-cu128-vs-cu130 mismatch + eager mode. First fix WSL memory in C:\Users\<you>\.wslconfig: [wsl2]\nmemory=56GB\nswap=16GB then wsl --shutdown. Inside Ubuntu 24.04 WSL2 with CUDA 12.8 + driver 581+: use a venv and pin Blackwell-correct wheels — uv pip install -U --pre vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/nightly (the nightly resolves torch 2.9.0+cu128 / sm_120 kernels; the plain PyPI install wrongly pulls cu130 torch and crashes). Serve a 14B AWQ with CUDA graphs ON (do NOT pass --enforce-eager): vllm serve /models/Qwen3-14B-AWQ --quantization awq_marlin --dtype float16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --attention-backend flashinfer --served-model-name qwen3-14b --port 8000. Measured on this exact rig: ~140 tok/s with CUDA graphs vs ~17 tok/s with --enforce-eager (8x). For a 32B AWQ raise to --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 and drop --max-model-len to ~6144 to fit KV in 32 GB; DeepSeek-R1-32B-AWQ sustained ~58 tok/s in a comparable config. This recipe also covers wave-1 vLLM server mode.

extras.name: aphrodite-wsl2-5090-anyquant-serve
extras.note: Aphrodite Engine v0.21.0 in WSL2 (Ubuntu 24.04, CUDA 12.8) when you need a quant format vLLM can't load (EXL3/MXFP4/QuIP#/AQLM) or richer samplers. Same.wslconfig memory bump as the vLLM recipe. In a venv: pip install -U aphrodite-engine; if the torch it pulls is cu130, force cu128 to match the sm_120 kernels: pip install --force-reinstall torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128. Launch the OpenAI server (defaults to port 2242): aphrodite run /models/Qwen3-14B-AWQ --quantization awq --dtype float16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-seqs 16; for an EXL3 model swap --quantization exl3. Blackwell NVFP4: if you have an NVFP4/ModelOpt checkpoint pass --quantization modelopt for the native Blackwell datatype (Marlin fallback on older arch). Test: curl http://localhost:2242/v1/chat/completions -d '{"model":"<served-name>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'. Throughput sits in the vLLM band (~140 tok/s 14B AWQ with CUDA graphs on); the reason to choose it is format breadth + samplers, not speed. AGPL-3.0 caveat applies.

extras.name: unsloth-qlora-14b-in-32gb-vram-windows-or-wsl2
extras.note: QLoRA-fine-tune a 14B in 32 GB VRAM on the 5090 (training, but the resulting LoRA serves through the engines above). Easiest path on Windows is WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 + CUDA 12.8 (Unsloth's Blackwell wheels target sm_120). In a venv: pip install unsloth; pip install --force-reinstall torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 if torch resolves to cu130. Exact config that fits 14B 4-bit + LoRA + paged optimizer in 32 GB: from unsloth import FastLanguageModel; model, tok = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(model_name='unsloth/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct', max_seq_length=4096, dtype=None, load_in_4bit=True); model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=16, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, target_modules=['q_proj','k_proj','v_proj','o_proj','gate_proj','up_proj','down_proj'], use_gradient_checkpointing='unsloth', random_state=3407). TrainingArguments: per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=8 (effective batch 16), learning_rate=2e-4, optim='paged_adamw_8bit', bf16=True, max_steps=500, warmup_steps=10, logging_steps=1, output_dir='outputs'. paged_adamw_8bit + use_gradient_checkpointing='unsloth' are the two levers that keep peak VRAM under 32 GB at 4k seq len; drop max_seq_length to 2048 or batch to 1 if you OOM on a larger base. Export: model.save_pretrained_gguf('out', tok, quantization_method='q4_k_m') to get a GGUF you can serve via llama-server/Ollama, or save_pretrained_merged for an EXL3/AWQ requant. Cross-platform reference only: on Apple Silicon use MLX-LM LoRA instead — not applicable to this rig.

extras.name: Blackwell-on-this-rig landmine checklist (cu128 vs cu130, eager mode, WDDM)
extras.note: Five recurring traps when serving on RTX 5090 / sm_120 / Win11, with fixes: (1) torch cu130 vs cu128 — Python engines (vLLM/Aphrodite/Unsloth) ship sm_120 kernels built for cu128, but the PyPI resolver grabs cu130 torch and crashes; fix by installing the nightly/cu128 wheel explicitly. (2) Eager mode — --enforce-eager (vLLM) drops you from ~140 to ~17 tok/s; always leave CUDA graphs on and prefer --attention-backend flashinfer. (3) Native-Windows reality — Ollama, llama.cpp (incl. router), and TabbyAPI build/run native; vLLM, Aphrodite, SGLang, and GPUStack-v2 workers are WSL2-only. (4) WSL2 VRAM/RAM — set memory=56GB in.wslconfig or large models OOM the WSL VM before the GPU. (5) Ollama '0 B VRAM' / CPU fallback on some Windows 5090 setups (ollama/ollama#13338) — update driver, confirm OLLAMA_LLM_LIBRARY not forced to cpu. Quantize KV (q8_0 / Q6) everywhere to stretch 32 GB; build llama.cpp with CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120.

research.domain: Quantization frameworks & formats — quant algorithms, tools, and weight formats (GGUF/GPTQ/AWQ/EXL/FP8/FP4) + the producer→format→consumer matrix. Wave 2 deep pass for an RTX 5090 (Blackwell sm_120, 32 GB VRAM) + 64 GB RAM Windows 11 local game studio.
research.notes: WAVE-2 SYNTHESIS — what the new engines change for this rig, and the one config takeaway that matters most. What changed this wave: the lane now has a clean, sourced PRODUCER->FORMAT->CONSUMER spine for FP4 on consumer Blackwell. The three additions close the gap wave 1 left open. (1) NVIDIA ModelOpt (v0.44.0, Apache-2.0) is the production PTQ that emits "unified HF checkpoints" in NVFP4/FP8 that vLLM (quantization="modelopt") and TensorRT-LLM consume directly — it is the calibration front-end for the entire NVIDIA FP4 stack. (2) torchao (v0.17.0, BSD-3-Clause) is the PyTorch-native mechanism underneath INT4/FP8/NVFP4 in vLLM, SGLang and especially Diffusers — for a ComfyUI/diffusion studio, torchao MXFP8/NVFP4 is the on-ramp to ~1.3-1.7x faster Blackwell image gen with near-identical convergence. (3) TensorRT-LLM (v1.2) is the fastest FP4 produce+serve runtime for Blackwell, but the honest finding is load-bearing: NVIDIA DEPRECATED native Windows in v0.18.0 — it is Linux/WSL2-only now. On a GeForce 5090 NVFP4 GEMM only unlocked at 0.20.0rc3 (the >=SM100 gate replaced the old "no GeForce Blackwell" block), and the proven real-world path is the nvidia/Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP4 checkpoint served via the official TRT-LLM container under WSL2. Net effect: this rig can now PRODUCE its own NVFP4 weights locally (ModelOpt or llm-compressor/torchao) and SERVE them at FP4 speeds (vLLM natively on Windows for AWQ/GPTQ; TRT-LLM in WSL2 for peak NVFP4). The format question is settled per-consumer: GGUF for llama.cpp partial-offload (the 64 GB RAM workhorse path), AWQ/GPTQ-Marlin or EXL3 for fits-in-32GB dense models, NVFP4 for the TRT-LLM/vLLM Blackwell fast lane, bitsandbytes NF4 only for QLoRA training (not serving). THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT CONFIG TAKEAWAY: On Blackwell, the CUDA TOOLKIT VERSION is the highest-leverage knob in this entire lane, and the correct answer is counter-intuitive — pin CUDA 12.8, not the newest. Benchmarked on a 5090, llama.cpp built with CUDA 12.8 + MMQ hits 5611 t/s prompt / 211 t/s gen on a Q4_K_M model; the SAME code built with CUDA 13.1 falls to 772 t/s / 121 t/s (5.7x slower prompt, 1.7x slower gen) because the Blackwell MMQ kernel segfaults under 13.1 and silently falls back to cuBLAS. The same cu128 pin governs the rest of the lane: vLLM needs torch 2.10.0+cu128 from its own wheel server (the PyPI resolver wrongly grabs cu130), Unsloth needs TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST="12.0" + triton>=3.3.1, and every build needs CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120. Second-order trap: CMake caches DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS in CMakeCache.txt, so you must `rm -rf build` (not just re-run cmake) when fixing a bad config or you keep the slow path forever. Get the toolkit pin right and everything in this lane runs at Blackwell speed; get it wrong and you lose 5x with no error message.

engines.model_formats: Produces: unified Hugging Face checkpoints (transformers + diffusers) in NVFP4, FP8, INT8, INT4. Consumed by TensorRT-LLM, TensorRT, vLLM (quantization="modelopt"), SGLang. Algorithms: SmoothQuant, AWQ, SVDQuant, Double Quantization, NVFP4 PTQ + QAT.

engines.summary: The production-grade PTQ/QAT front-end for NVIDIA's FP4 stack, rebranded from 'TensorRT Model Optimizer' to 'Model Optimizer' in Dec 2025. Implements SmoothQuant, AWQ, SVDQuant, double-quant and native NVFP4 (E2M1, block-16, FP8 scales) and FP8 calibration, then exports unified HF checkpoints deployable in TensorRT-LLM, TensorRT, vLLM and SGLang without re-conversion. On this rig it is the canonical way to LOCALLY produce NVFP4/FP8 weights — `pip install -U nvidia-modelopt[hf]` then `python hf_ptq.py --pyt_ckpt_path <model> --qformat nvfp4 --export_path out` — closing the loop so the 5090 isn't dependent on third-party FP4 uploads. Default calibration mixes cnn_dailymail + nemotron-post-training-dataset-v2 (128-512 samples). Accuracy-tuned variants (nvfp4_mlp_only / nvfp4_experts_only) recover quality on sensitive layers.

extras.name: llama-cpp-blackwell-cuda128-build-and-serve
extras.note: THE Blackwell build recipe — pin CUDA 12.8, never 13.x (5.7x perf trap). Build: `rm -rf build` (CMakeCache caches FORCE_CUBLAS — re-running cmake won't clear it) then `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS=OFF -DCUDAToolkit_ROOT=/usr/local/cuda-12.8` (Windows: point -DCUDAToolkit_ROOT to the v12.8 install and use Visual Studio 2022 generator) then `cmake --build build --config Release -j`. Verify MMQ is active. Serve a 30-70B MoE with partial offload on 32GB VRAM + 64GB RAM: `llama-server -m model.gguf -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 24 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080`. --n-cpu-moe N keeps N expert layers in CPU RAM (the 64GB lever) while attention/dense stay on GPU; FA + q8_0 KV nearly halves KV memory at 32k ctx. Benchmark (5090, Q4_K_M, CUDA 12.8 + MMQ): 5611 t/s prompt, 211 t/s gen — vs CUDA 13.1 + cuBLAS 772/121. KNOWN BUG: some sm_120 MXFP4 kernel paths fail ptxas ('mma with block scale'); if MXFP4 GGUF won't build, use Q4_K_M/Q5_K_M/Q6_K instead (issue ggml-org/llama.cpp#19662).

extras.note: vLLM on the 5090 in WSL2 (Ubuntu). Install from vLLM's OWN wheel server — PyPI wrongly resolves torch to cu130; you need cu128: `uv pip install -U vllm --torch-backend=cu128` (pulls torch 2.10.0+cu128, vllm ~0.18.x). Serve a 14B AWQ that fits in 32GB: `vllm serve /path/Qwen3-14B-AWQ --quantization awq_marlin --dtype float16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --attention-backend flashinfer --swap-space 4 --port 11436 --served-model-name qwen3-14b`. CUDA graphs (default — do NOT pass --enforce-eager) are the whole ballgame: ~140 tok/s WITH graphs vs ~17 tok/s eager. WSL2 stability fixes that actually matter on Blackwell: WSL2 >= 2.7.0; remove Tailscale from WSL2; hard-mask nvidia-cdi-refresh; add a ~45s boot delay to CUDA services or graph capture intermittently fails. For NVFP4 weights, swap to `--quantization modelopt` against a ModelOpt-exported checkpoint.

extras.name: vllm-native-windows-awq-no-wsl
extras.note: vLLM WITHOUT WSL2 when you want to stay native-Windows (simpler than TRT-LLM, which is WSL2-only). Working combo reported on a 5090: torch 2.9.0+cu128 (or 2.10.0+cu128) + matching vllm wheel. Create a clean venv, then `pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128` and verify `python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.get_device_capability())"` prints (12, 0). Launch AWQ/GPTQ models with awq_marlin/gptq_marlin kernels and `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --max-model-len 16384`. Native Windows vLLM is the pragmatic 'serve quantized models with one command, no Linux container' lane for this studio; reserve WSL2 for NVFP4-via-TRT-LLM only.

extras.name: modelopt-produce-nvfp4-checkpoint-locally
extras.note: Produce your OWN NVFP4 weights on the 5090 (no dependence on third-party FP4 uploads). `pip install -U nvidia-modelopt[hf]` then from the llm_ptq example dir `pip install -r requirements.txt`. Quantize + export a unified HF checkpoint: `python hf_ptq.py --pyt_ckpt_path <hf-model-or-path> --qformat nvfp4 --export_path./qwen3-14b-nvfp4 --calib_size 512`. For accuracy on sensitive layers use `--qformat nvfp4_mlp_only` or `nvfp4_experts_only` instead of plain nvfp4. Default calibration = cnn_dailymail + nemotron-post-training-dataset-v2. The exported dir loads directly: in vLLM `LLM(model='./qwen3-14b-nvfp4', quantization='modelopt')`; in TRT-LLM `LLM(model='./qwen3-14b-nvfp4')`. Match --tp to your serving layout (1 for single 5090). Calibration runs fine on Windows; serve the result with native-Windows vLLM (modelopt) or WSL2 TRT-LLM.

extras.name: tensorrt-llm-wsl2-nvfp4-fast-lane
extras.note: Peak NVFP4 serving on a GeForce 5090 — WSL2-only (native Windows TRT-LLM is deprecated since v0.18.0). Prereqs: Windows 11 + WSL2 (Ubuntu) + recent NVIDIA driver (580.95.05 Open verified) + nvidia-container-toolkit inside WSL2. Pull the official NGC TensorRT-LLM container (CUDA 12.8.1 base) and run a pre-quantized NVFP4 model: `nvidia/Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP4` is confirmed working ('Recommended! Solid performance'). Simplest path is the linked Docker Compose: `docker compose up -d` (TRT-LLM API on :8000, Open WebUI on :3000; bearer token 'tensorrt_llm'). FIRST RUN builds the TensorRT engine = 10-30 min (cached after). NVFP4 GEMM requires TRT-LLM >= 0.20.0rc3 on GeForce (sm_120); v1.2 is current. Feed it ModelOpt-produced NVFP4 checkpoints (see modelopt recipe) or HF FP4 uploads. Use this lane only for a pinned high-throughput target — for ad-hoc local chat, vLLM/llama.cpp are far less ceremony.

extras.name: unsloth-qlora-14b-32gb-blackwell
extras.note: QLoRA a 14B in 32GB VRAM on the 5090 (the studio's LoRA/style fine-tune path). Blackwell env: `export TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST="12.0"`, triton>=3.3.1, and if pulling vLLM for inference `uv pip install -U vllm --torch-backend=cu128`. Install `pip install unsloth` (Docker image unsloth/unsloth needs no Blackwell variant). Config: `model, tok = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(model_name='unsloth/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-bnb-4bit', max_seq_length=2048, load_in_4bit=True, dtype=None)` then `model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=16, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, target_modules=['q_proj','k_proj','v_proj','o_proj','gate_proj','up_proj','down_proj'], use_gradient_checkpointing='unsloth')`. Trainer args for 32GB: `per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=8, optim='paged_adamw_8bit', learning_rate=2e-4, bf16=True, max_seq_length=2048` (paged_adamw_8bit offloads optimizer state to the 64GB system RAM — the lever that keeps a 14B QLoRA inside 32GB). WSL2: set >=16GB memory in.wslconfig; build xformers with TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0 + --no-build-isolation. bitsandbytes NF4 is the underlying 4-bit (training only — do not serve NF4).

extras.name: exllamav3-exl3-tabbyapi-5090-serve
extras.note: EXL3 (ExLlamaV3) via tabbyAPI — best-quality single-GPU INT-ish quant that fits 32GB, OpenAI-compatible, runs native Windows. Install in a cu128 venv: `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128`, build/install exllamav3 for sm_120 (TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0 if compiling), then clone theroyallab/tabbyAPI and `pip install -r requirements.txt`. In tabbyAPI config.yml set `model_dir` to your EXL3 weights, pick a bpw that fits (e.g. a 32B at ~4.0-4.5 bpw sits comfortably in 32GB with room for context), and set `cache_mode: Q8` or `Q6` to shrink the KV cache, `max_seq_len: 32768`. Launch `python main.py`; OpenAI API on :5000. EXL3's variable-bitrate quant gives better quality-per-GB than fixed GPTQ at the same size — the go-to for 'largest dense model that still fits one 5090 at high quality'. Grab community EXL3 weights from HF (e.g. *-EXL3 repos).

extras.name: torchao-diffusers-blackwell-mxfp8-nvfp4
extras.note: Speed up local ComfyUI/Diffusers image gen on the 5090 (the studio's real diffusion workload). Install cu128 torch + torchao: `pip install torch torchao --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128` (NVFP4/MXFP8 kernels are Blackwell-gated and need CUDA 12.8+; NVFP4 QAT landed torchao v0.14.1, MXFP8 matured through v0.17.0). In a Diffusers pipeline quantize the transformer in place: `from torchao.quantization import quantize_, Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig; quantize_(pipe.transformer, Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig())` (FP8) — or the MXFP8/NVFP4 configs per the blog for max speed. Reproducible Blackwell numbers: ~1.26x e2e with MXFP8, ~1.68x with NVFP4, near-identical image quality vs BF16. This is the cleanest path to faster local art generation without leaving PyTorch; torchao is also what vLLM/SGLang import under the hood, so the same install serves double duty.

extras.name: format-to-consumer-matrix-this-rig
extras.note: PRODUCER->FORMAT->CONSUMER decision matrix for this 5090 rig. (1) GGUF -> llama.cpp/ik_llama.cpp: the 64GB-RAM partial-offload workhorse; produce with `llama-quantize in.gguf out.gguf Q4_K_M` (or Q5_K_M/Q6_K; avoid MXFP4 GGUF on sm_120 until ptxas bug #19662 clears). Best for 30-70B MoE bigger than VRAM via --n-cpu-moe. (2) AWQ or GPTQ -> vLLM (awq_marlin/gptq_marlin, native Windows) for dense models that FIT in 32GB at ~140 tok/s. (3) EXL3 -> tabbyAPI: best quality-per-GB single-GPU, native Windows, variable bpw. (4) NVFP4 -> vLLM (quantization='modelopt', native Windows) OR TensorRT-LLM (WSL2-only, peak speed); produce with NVIDIA ModelOpt or llm-compressor/torchao. (5) bitsandbytes NF4 -> training only (QLoRA via Unsloth), never serve. Rule of thumb: fits-in-VRAM dense -> AWQ/EXL3 native Windows; too-big MoE -> GGUF partial offload; want maximum FP4 throughput on a pinned model -> NVFP4 + TRT-LLM in WSL2; fine-tuning -> NF4. Every CUDA build pins 12.8 + sm_120.

research.notes: WAVE-2 SYNTHESIS (Attention backends & GPU kernels, RTX 5090 / sm_120 / Win11). The single load-bearing fact this wave establishes: consumer Blackwell (sm_120) is a DIFFERENT, NON-cross-compatible ISA from datacenter Blackwell (sm_100/sm_103). The 12.x family (sm_120 = RTX 5090/5080/5070, sm_121 = GB10/DGX Spark) uses `mma.sync.aligned...block_scale` and lacks the `tcgen05` instructions + TMEM that sm_100 kernels are built on. So "Blackwell support" in a repo's README is NOT automatically 5090 support — you must verify sm_120 specifically. The three new engines split exactly along this fault line: (1) ThunderKittens 2.0 explicitly lists `SM120` as an ARCH build target — it is the one new engine that genuinely targets the 5090, but it is a Linux-first CUDA DSL for kernel authors, not a drop-in runtime, so its studio_fit is low. (2) NATTEN's fast FNA/FMHA kernels are Hopper(sm90)+Blackwell-DATACENTER(sm100) only; on a 5090 it silently falls back to the CUTLASS FNA path (slower) or the pure-PyTorch Flex backend, and it ships Linux-only wheels (Windows = experimental WindowsBuilder.bat from source) — so it's a Linux/WSL2 tool for diffusion-transformer/video sparse-attention, useful to the studio's ComfyUI side but not a Windows-native win. (3) trtllm-gen FMHA (the NVIDIA fused-MHA cubins TRT-LLM and FlashInfer consume via flashinfer-cubin) is the cautionary tale: through mid-2026 flashinfer-cubin shipped ONLY Sm100a/Sm100f/Sm103a cubins, and on a 5090 the loader fell through to a wrong-arch cubin via family compat and emitted GARBAGE TOKENS with no error (flashinfer #3294) — the fix path (SM120 patches + compute_120f, CUDA 13.0) lands ~39 tok/s native FP4 but is patch-required, not stock. What this CHANGES for the rig: do NOT chase the trtllm-gen/NVFP4-MoE FMHA path on stock wheels — it's broken-by-silence on sm_120; prefer the FlashInfer *standard* attention backend (its CUTLASS/AOT kernels DO work on sm_120 and give vLLM +8%) or, for diffusion, SageAttention (the real studio win: ~35% faster sampling, native-Windows prebuilt wheel). THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT CONFIG TAKEAWAY: pin CUDA 12.8 and arch 120 everywhere, and treat FP8/FP4/trtllm-gen as the danger zone. Three traps stack: (a) build llama.cpp/anything with CUDA Toolkit 13.x instead of 12.8 → up to 5x slowdown + MXFP4 sm_120 PTX compile failures; keep FORCE_CUBLAS OFF so MMQ kernels stay on. (b) On Windows-via-WSL2, dxgkrnl does NOT expose Blackwell FP8/FP4 tensor cores → FP8 quant runs ~3x SLOWER than the AWQ-Marlin INT4 path, the opposite of bare-metal intuition; choose `awq_marlin` over FP8 on WSL2. (c) sm_120 needs PyTorch 2.9+ cu128/cu130 (or nightly for the newest kernels) — stable PT compiled only to sm_90 emits "no kernel image available." Net: the studio's bread-and-butter (llama.cpp partial-MoE offload using 64 GB RAM, SageAttention in ComfyUI on native Windows, vLLM-in-WSL2 with AWQ-Marlin + FlashInfer, Unsloth QLoRA of a 14B in 32 GB) all works TODAY with the right pins — but every one of them has a version/arch landmine that the recipes below defuse explicitly.

engines.name: ThunderKittens 2.0
engines.commercial_notes: Permissive MIT — free for commercial use including closed-source products. No attribution burden beyond the license file.
engines.platforms: Linux (primary). No Windows build instructions provided; Linux-focused setup. WSL2 is the practical Windows path.
engines.accelerators: NVIDIA Hopper (sm_90) and Blackwell. Build ARCH target supports SM80/SM90/SM100/SM103/SM120, so consumer Blackwell sm_120 (RTX 5090) IS a listed target. Ampere no longer actively supported.
engines.model_formats: N/A — a kernel-authoring library, not a model runtime. Emits BF16 / FP8 (MXFP8) / NVFP4 GEMM + attention kernels you compile and link.
engines.optimization_for: Hand-written tile-primitive attention + GEMM kernels at near-cuDNN / near-cuBLAS speed; FlashAttention-3-style fwd/bwd, linear attention (LoLCATS), sliding-window (Based), MXFP8/NVFP4 GEMM.
engines.multi_gpu: Yes — supports NVLink data transfer and NVSwitch acceleration for multi-GPU ops (datacenter-oriented; not relevant to a single 5090).
engines.speed_note: On B200: attention fwd/bwd at near-cuDNN speed and up to 2x faster than FA3-on-H100; BF16/MXFP8/NVFP4 GEMM matching or beating cuBLAS. The headline benchmarks are all B200 (sm_100); no published sm_120 (5090) numbers — consumer Blackwell has far less FP4/tensor-mem throughput than B200, so do not expect B200 ratios on a 5090.
engines.summary: A header-only CUDA DSL of 16x16 tile primitives for writing attention/GEMM kernels that hit near-vendor-library speed without raw PTX. v2.0 (Jan 2026) refactored internals (removed redundant memory fences ~20-30 TFLOP/s, fixed NVFP4 tensor-core pipelining ~500 TFLOP/s, assembler cleanups) and added full Blackwell support with MXFP8 + NVFP4 precision and SOTA GEMM kernels. Crucially for this rig, the test/build ARCH enum includes SM120, so it can target the RTX 5090 directly (unlike NATTEN's fast kernels or the trtllm-gen cubins, which are sm_100-only). It is NOT an inference server or a drop-in backend — it is the layer you reach for when you need a custom fused kernel (a novel attention variant, a studio-specific GEMM shape) and the off-the-shelf libraries don't have it. For a single-human game studio that mostly consumes existing engines, that's a narrow but real niche; high ceiling, requires CUDA kernel skills.

best_for.purpose: Authoring a custom fused attention/GEMM kernel for sm_120 when no off-the-shelf kernel fits
MXFP8 / NVFP4 GEMM experimentation on Blackwell
Research into FlashAttention-4-class or linear-attention kernels

engines.name: NATTEN
engines.language: CUDA / C++ with PyTorch bindings (Python API)
engines.commercial_notes: MIT — commercial-friendly. Note the academic Neighborhood Attention method itself is unencumbered; the library is MIT.
engines.platforms: Linux: prebuilt wheels (x86-64 + aarch64). Windows: experimental, build-from-source only via WindowsBuilder.bat ('not regularly tested'). macOS: PyTorch Flex backend only (cross-platform reference). PyPI sdist falls back to PyTorch Flex Attention if libnatten isn't built.
engines.accelerators: NVIDIA since Maxwell (sm_50). FAST native FNA/FMHA kernels: Hopper (sm_90) and Blackwell DATACENTER (sm_100, sm_103) ONLY. Consumer Blackwell sm_120 (RTX 5090) is NOT a native-kernel target — it falls back to the CUTLASS FNA backend or the experimental Flex backend.
engines.model_formats: N/A — a PyTorch attention operator library (FP16/BF16 tensors). Plugs into diffusion/video transformers, ViTs, segmentation models.
engines.optimization_for: Multi-dimensional sparse / neighborhood (sliding-window) attention — 1D/2D/3D, dilated, causal, strided, block-sparse — with speedups proportional to the FLOP reduction over dense cuDNN/FA3.
engines.multi_gpu: Inherits PyTorch (DDP/FSDP); the kernels themselves are single-GPU operators.
engines.speed_note: On H100/B200 the Hopper/Blackwell FNA kernels deliver speedups proportional to the FLOP reduction vs cuDNN/FA3 (large for small windows). On a 5090 you do NOT get those kernels — you get the CUTLASS FNA path (still a real fused kernel, sm_50+, decent) or the Flex fallback (slowest). Benchmark on the rig before assuming a win.
engines.summary: The reference library for sparse/neighborhood attention — sliding-window self-attention and its dilated/causal/strided/block-sparse variants — shipping Fused Neighborhood Attention (FNA) and FMHA kernels for every NVIDIA arch since Maxwell, plus dedicated Hopper and Blackwell-datacenter native kernels. The 0.21.x line added even-sized windows, strided NA, block-sparse NA, a NATTEN Simulator, and out-of-kernel token-permutation Hopper/Blackwell FNA. For this rig the honest read: the fast kernels are sm_90/sm_100, NOT sm_120, so on a 5090 you run CUTLASS-FNA or Flex; and there are no Windows wheels (build from source, experimental). Where it earns its place in a game studio is the diffusion/video side — neighborhood attention is heavily used in high-res image and video diffusion transformers (the kind of work that runs in ComfyUI / a WSL2 training box), where windowing real high-res frames slashes attention FLOPs. Treat it as a Linux/WSL2 diffusion-transformer tool, not a Windows LLM-inference backend.

best_for.purpose: Sparse/windowed attention in high-res image & video diffusion transformers (ComfyUI / WSL2 training)
ViT / segmentation / dense-prediction models using neighborhood attention
Cutting attention FLOPs on long 2D/3D sequences where a sliding window is acceptable

engines.summary: Not a standalone product you install but the NVIDIA-authored fused-MHA cubin layer baked into TensorRT-LLM and re-exposed to the open ecosystem through flashinfer-cubin (FlashInfer's TllmGenFmha runner). On datacenter Blackwell it is the top-tier attention path. The reason it appears here as a WARNING engine: on this rig's RTX 5090 (sm_120) it is the single most dangerous attention path because sm_120 is a different ISA family (no tcgen05/TMEM; uses mma.sync block-scale) and stock cubins only target sm_100/sm_103. flashinfer-cubin 0.6.11 shipped zero sm_120/121 cubins, so on a 5090 the cubin loader silently selected a wrong-arch binary and produced degenerate output — both the precompiled and JIT FP4-MoE paths broken (flashinfer #3294, NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM #11799). A fix exists (PR #3302; CUTLASS #3096 documents the SM120-patch + compute_120f recovery at ~39 tok/s FP4) but it is patch-and-rebuild territory. Operational guidance for this rig: do NOT force the trtllm-gen / TllmGenFmha backend; use FlashInfer's standard attention backend (which DOES work on sm_120) or another backend entirely. Listed so the KB explicitly steers around the trap.

extras.name: RECIPE-llamacpp-blackwell-build-cu128-sm120
extras.note: llama.cpp native-Windows Blackwell build (THE wave-1 workhorse on this rig). LANDMINE FIRST: build with CUDA Toolkit 12.8, NOT 13.x — CUDA 13 causes crashes/up-to-5x slowdown and MXFP4 sm_120 PTX compile failures (llama.cpp #19662). Steps (Win11 native, VS2022 + CUDA 12.8 installed): `git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp; cd llama.cpp` then `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS=OFF` then `cmake --build build --config Release -j`. CRITICAL: keep FORCE_CUBLAS OFF so the MMQ integer kernels stay enabled (CUDA 12.8 + MMQ is the optimal Blackwell combo); if you EVER built with FORCE_CUBLAS=ON, delete the whole build/ dir before rebuilding or MMQ stays disabled and you eat a massive slowdown. Run a dense 14-32B fully on GPU: `build\bin\Release\llama-server.exe -m model.gguf -ngl 99 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080`. The `-fa` (flash attention) flag uses llama.cpp's own fused-attention kernels (no external dep). For a big MoE that doesn't fit in 32 GB, exploit the 64 GB system RAM with partial expert offload — see RECIPE-llamacpp-moe-cpu-offload-5090.

extras.name: RECIPE-llamacpp-moe-cpu-offload-5090-64gbRAM
extras.note: llama.cpp MoE partial CPU offload — the move that turns 32 GB VRAM + 64 GB RAM into a big-MoE box. Strategy: put all dense/attention layers on the GPU (`-ngl 99`) and push the bulky-but-sparsely-activated MoE expert FFN tensors to CPU RAM with `--n-cpu-moe N` (newer flag) or the older `--cpu-moe` (offload ALL experts). Tune N down from the layer count until VRAM is ~90% full. Verified data points on a 5090: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE Q4_K_XL fits fully in ~25.6 GB VRAM and hits ~236 tok/s gen with `llama-server --cpu-moe` (it's A3B = only 3B active, so CPU experts barely hurt); the same 32 GB card can hold a 262k-token context on that model without spilling. For a model where experts won't all fit, e.g. a 100B+ MoE: `llama-server -m moe.gguf -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 24 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 -t 16` (-t = physical cores on the Core Ultra 9; lower --n-cpu-moe = more experts on GPU = faster until you OOM). Rule of thumb: A3B-class MoEs offload almost for free; high-active-param MoEs degrade more per offloaded expert. KV-cache q8_0 roughly halves cache VRAM with negligible quality loss — essential for long context on 32 GB.

extras.name: RECIPE-sageattention-comfyui-windows-native-5090
extras.note: SageAttention 2.2.0 on native-Windows ComfyUI for the RTX 5090 — the BIGGEST single studio win in this lane (~30-35% faster diffusion sampling, no WSL2 needed). SageAttention 2.2 is wave-1 but the Blackwell/Windows wheel is the payload. Path A (prebuilt, fastest): grab the community wheel matching your exact PyTorch nightly, e.g. `sageattention-2.2.0+cu128.torch2.11-cp311-cp311-win_amd64.whl` (built against torch 2.11.0.dev20260127). Install into the ComfyUI portable python: `.\python_embeded\python.exe -m pip install sageattention-2.2.0+cu128.torch2.11-cp311-cp311-win_amd64.whl`. The wheel version MUST match your installed PyTorch nightly date or it won't load — if your nightly differs, rebuild from source. RTX 50-series needs PyTorch 2.11 nightly (stable PT only ships sm_90). WIRING (do NOT use the `--use-sage-attention` global flag — its Triton backend emits BLACK/garbage output on Qwen/Wan): instead install ComfyUI-KJNodes, add a 'Patch Sage Attention' node, set backend to `sageattn_qk_int8_pv_fp16_cuda`. Use the cu130 wheel variant only if you need FP4-model support via comfy-kitchen. Path B (build from source) requires the PyTorch header patch: edit `<venv>\Lib\site-packages\torch\include\torch\csrc\dynamo\compiled_autograd.h` ~lines 1135-1136 and comment out the `::std::string` conditional to clear the MSVC C2872 error, then `pip install -e.`. License: Apache-2.0.

extras.name: RECIPE-vllm-wsl2-5090-awq-marlin-flashinfer
extras.note: vLLM on a 5090 via WSL2 — verified working config (CUDA graphs DO work on sm_120 under WSL2 2.7.0, long believed broken). Env: vLLM 0.17.1+, CUDA 12.8 (driver 581.80+), WSL2 2.7.0+, PyTorch with sm_120 (cu128/cu130 wheel or nightly). Serve a 14B AWQ: `python3 -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model /path/Qwen3-14B-AWQ --quantization awq_marlin --dtype float16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --max-model-len 8192 --port 11436 --served-model-name qwen3-14b --attention-backend flashinfer --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --swap-space 4`. Benchmarks: ~140 tok/s with CUDA graphs vs ~17 tok/s in --enforce-eager (so DON'T force eager) vs ~111 tok/s Ollama baseline; the flashinfer attention backend adds ~+8%. TWO LANDMINES: (1) Choose `awq_marlin` (INT4) over FP8 — on WSL2 dxgkrnl does NOT expose Blackwell FP8/FP4 tensor cores, so FP8 runs ~3x SLOWER, the opposite of bare-metal. (2) Do NOT force the trtllm-gen path / NVFP4-MoE backend on sm_120 (garbage output, flashinfer #3294); the STANDARD flashinfer attention backend is fine but can fail head_size checks on some models (e.g. Gemma-4 #40677) — fall back to the default backend if a model rejects it. WSL2 stability: mask nvidia-cdi-refresh, add boot delays to CUDA services, drop Tailscale to avoid init races. Push --gpu-memory-utilization to 0.90-0.92 for a tighter fit.

extras.name: RECIPE-flashinfer-install-cu128-sm120-AOT-source
extras.note: FlashInfer (wave-1) on sm_120 — install + the source-build escape hatch for consumer Blackwell. Latest is 0.6.12 (CUDA 12.6/12.8/13.0/13.1). Stock install for cu128: `pip install flashinfer-python flashinfer-cubin` then `pip install flashinfer-jit-cache --index-url https://flashinfer.ai/whl/cu128`; verify with `flashinfer show-config`. IMPORTANT sm_120 caveat: the STANDARD attention kernels (CUTLASS/AOT) work on the 5090 and are what vLLM uses for its +8% — but flashinfer-cubin's trtllm-gen FMHA + NVFP4-MoE cubins are sm_100/sm_103 only and silently emit garbage on sm_120 (#3294, fixed by PR #3302 in the 0.6.x line — confirm your version >= the fix or avoid the FP4-MoE path). If you need every kernel AOT-compiled natively for sm_120, build from source with the family-compat arch list: `export FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST="7.5 8.0 8.9 9.0a 10.0a 10.3a 11.0a 12.0f"` then `python -m flashinfer.aot` then `pip install -e. --no-build-isolation`. The `12.0f` (family-specific, forward-compatible within 12.x) is the token that gets you valid RTX 5090 kernels; CUDA 13.0 + compute_120f is the validated recovery path that restored native FP4 (~39 tok/s) per CUTLASS #3096.

extras.name: RECIPE-unsloth-qlora-14b-32gb-paged-adamw8bit
extras.note: Unsloth QLoRA of a 14B inside 32 GB VRAM (the studio's LoRA/style-finetune path; runs in WSL2 or native Win). NVIDIA's own RTX-5090 reference config: Alpaca, 4-bit QLoRA on ALL linear layers, rank=32, per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=4. Skeleton: `from unsloth import FastLanguageModel; model, tok = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(model_name='unsloth/Qwen3-14B-bnb-4bit', max_seq_length=2048, dtype=None, load_in_4bit=True); model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=32, lora_alpha=32, target_modules=['q_proj','k_proj','v_proj','o_proj','gate_proj','up_proj','down_proj'], use_gradient_checkpointing='unsloth')`. Trainer args: `per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, optim='paged_adamw_8bit', learning_rate=2e-4, bf16=True, max_seq_length=2048`. The paged_adamw_8bit optimizer (needs bitsandbytes) pages optimizer state to the 64 GB system RAM, which is what keeps a 14B QLoRA inside 32 GB. Headroom is tight: a 14B QLoRA SFT fits comfortably; GRPO/RL on a 14B climbs to 22-28 GB and leaves little room for long sequences — keep max_seq_length modest (≤2048-4096) for RL, raise it for plain SFT. Unsloth = up to 2x faster / ~70% less VRAM than vanilla HF. Install needs PyTorch with sm_120 (cu128/cu130 or nightly) + matching bitsandbytes; on stock-PT you'll hit 'no kernel image available for sm_120'.

extras.name: RECIPE-thunderkittens-build-sm120
extras.note: ThunderKittens 2.0 build/use for the RTX 5090 (kernel authoring — only when you need a custom fused kernel). Header-only, MIT, needs CUDA 12.8+ and a C++20 compiler (GCC-11+; Linux/WSL2 — no Windows-native build path documented). Setup: `git clone https://github.com/HazyResearch/ThunderKittens`, then in your kernel's source `#include "kittens.cuh"`. Build kernels/tests targeting consumer Blackwell with the SM120 arch (the ARCH enum supports SM80/SM90/SM100/SM103/SM120): e.g. `make ARCH=SM120` in a kernel dir, or for nvcc `-arch=sm_120a` / `-gencode arch=compute_120,code=sm_120`. The shipped headline kernels (FA-style fwd/bwd, LoLCATS linear attn, Based sliding-window, MXFP8/NVFP4 GEMM) are tuned and benchmarked on B200 (sm_100) — on a 5090 they compile for sm_120 but expect far lower FP4/tensor-mem throughput than the B200 numbers; profile before trusting. Use this only to author a fused kernel the off-the-shelf libraries (FlashInfer/cuDNN/SageAttention) don't provide for your shape — it is a DSL, not a runtime, so it never replaces llama.cpp/vLLM for ordinary inference.

extras.name: RECIPE-natten-wsl2-cutlass-fallback-5090
extras.note: NATTEN on the 5090 for diffusion/video sparse attention — Linux/WSL2 path (Windows wheels do not exist). In WSL2 Ubuntu with PyTorch>=2.7 cu128/cu130 for sm_120: `pip install natten==0.21.6+torch2110cu130 -f https://whl.natten.org` (pick the cu/torch tag matching your PyTorch — cu126/cu128/cu130, torch 2.10/2.11). REALITY for this rig: the prebuilt libnatten ships fast FNA/FMHA kernels for Hopper sm_90 and Blackwell-DATACENTER sm_100 only — there is NO native sm_120 kernel, so on a 5090 NATTEN runs the CUTLASS-FNA backend (real fused kernel, sm_50+, works but slower than the sm_100 path) or, via the plain `pip install natten` sdist, the pure-PyTorch Flex backend (slowest fallback). To force/inspect the backend use the NATTEN Profiler/Simulator and pick CUTLASS-FNA for sm_120. Native Windows: only `WindowsBuilder.bat install CUDA_ARCH=12.0` from source, explicitly experimental and untested — prefer WSL2. Best applied to high-res image/video diffusion transformers in ComfyUI-on-WSL2 where windowed attention cuts FLOPs; do not expect it to accelerate LLM inference.

research.domain: Training & fine-tuning engines (full / LoRA / QLoRA / RLHF / DPO / RL post-training) — Wave 2 deep pass
research.notes: WAVE-2 SYNTHESIS — what the new engines change for this rig, and the one config takeaway. WHAT CHANGED: Wave 1 covered the SFT/LoRA/QLoRA layer (Unsloth, Axolotl, LLaMA-Factory, TRL+PEFT) and the distributed-training plumbing (DeepSpeed, Megatron, FSDP2, NeMo). Wave 2 adds the RL POST-TRAINING layer that became dominant in 2026: veRL (the de-facto standard — v0.8.0, Jun 1 2026, FSDP/FSDP2/Megatron training x vLLM/SGLang rollout, PPO/GRPO/GSPO/DAPO/RLOO/REINFORCE++/PRIME), OpenRLHF (v0.10.3, the Ray+vLLM+DeepSpeed production path, async agentic RL, 70B+ full tuning), and torchtitan (v0.2.2, Meta's PyTorch-native 4D-parallel pre-training successor to the now-deprecated torchtune). These three are the answer to "how do I do GRPO/DPO/RLHF locally," which wave-1 SFT engines do not cover. For THIS single-5090 rig the realistic RL workload is small: GRPO/DPO on a 0.5B-7B policy with a colocated vLLM rollout in WSL2, or DPO via TRL/Unsloth (cheapest path, no Ray). veRL/OpenRLHF shine at 8xGPU scale; on one 32 GB card they are runnable-but-cramped and exist here mainly as the correct tool when you rent cloud GPUs — local single-GPU GRPO of a 1.5-7B model is the practical ceiling, with rollout colocated at gpu_memory_utilization~0.4-0.5 and FSDP CPU-offload eating into the 64 GB system RAM. torchtitan is pre-training-first and overkill for a LoRA studio; it earns a spot as reference for from-scratch small-model runs, not daily use. THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT CONFIG TAKEAWAY: On Blackwell/sm_120 everything is gated on ONE thing — a CUDA-12.8 (cu128) PyTorch >= 2.7.0 base, installed LAST. PyTorch 2.7.0 was the first stable wheel with native sm_120 (cuDNN/NCCL/CUTLASS/Triton 3.3 upgraded); torch 2.9.0+cu128 is the confirmed working base for vLLM on a 5090 as of mid-2026. Every recipe in this lane reduces to: (1) Win11 + driver R570+, (2) torch==2.9.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128, (3) install framework deps with --no-deps or torch installed last so a stray requirements.txt cannot drag in a cu126/sm_90 wheel that silently CPU-falls-back or throws "sm_120 not compatible," (4) pin numpy<2 and triton>=3.3.1. Get the cu128 base right and Unsloth runs Windows-native; veRL/OpenRLHF/Axolotl/LLaMA-Factory run cleanly in WSL2 (their Ray/DeepSpeed/vLLM/Triton stacks are Linux-first). Get it wrong and you waste a day on a green-looking install that uses the CPU. For the studio's actual workload, Unsloth Windows-native QLoRA is the daily driver (14B in ~8.5 GB, 32B fits in 26 GB), TRL/Unsloth DPO covers preference tuning without Ray, and veRL-in-WSL2 is the escalation path for real GRPO.

engines.summary: The de-facto standard open-source RL post-training framework in 2026 and the wave-1-flagged #1 must-have. extras.name: blackwell-cu128-torch-base-the-one-prerequisite
extras.note: THE prerequisite every recipe below depends on. RTX 5090 / sm_120 needs PyTorch >= 2.7.0 built for CUDA 12.8 (cu128) — torch 2.7.0 was the FIRST stable wheel with native Blackwell (cuDNN/NCCL/CUTLASS/Triton 3.3 upgraded). As of mid-2026 torch 2.9.0+cu128 is the confirmed working base on a 5090 (vLLM forum). Win11 host: NVIDIA driver R570+ (CUDA 12.8 needs R570 or higher). RULE: install torch LAST so no stray requirements.txt drags in a cu126/sm_90 wheel that silently CPU-falls-back. Windows-native (for Unsloth): `python -m venv.venv &&.venv\Scripts\activate; pip install --upgrade pip; pip install torch==2.9.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128; pip install numpy==1.26.4 "triton>=3.3.1"`. Verify: `python -c "import torch;print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.get_device_capability())"` MUST print cu12.8 and (12,0) — if it prints (9,0) or warns 'sm_120 not compatible', the wrong wheel won. WSL2 base (for veRL/OpenRLHF/Axolotl/LLaMA-Factory/vLLM): `wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04` on the host, install NVIDIA Container Toolkit for Docker-in-WSL, then inside Ubuntu use the same torch==2.9.0 cu128 install. Pin numpy<2 (numpy 2.x breaks frameworks with un-rebuilt C extensions).

extras.name: unsloth-windows-native-qlora-14b-32gb-daily-driver
extras.note:
THE studio daily driver — QLoRA fine-tune a 14B (or up to 32B) in 32 GB, Windows-native (no WSL2 needed for Unsloth). Install on the cu128 base from the recipe above: `pip install unsloth unsloth_zoo bitsandbytes; pip install -U "triton>=3.3.1"` (Unsloth ships Blackwell-tuned kernels; if you hit xformers issues, `set TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0` then build xformers from source). VRAM budget (Unsloth official, QLoRA 4-bit minimums): 7B=5GB, 8B=6GB, 14B=8.5GB, 32B=26GB, 70B=41GB(too big) — so a 14B leaves ~23 GB headroom for long context, a 32B just fits. Config:
```python
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel
import torch
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Qwen3-14B-bnb-4bit", # or any unsloth 4bit repo max_seq_length=4096, # 14B leaves room to push to 8192+ dtype=None, # auto bf16 on Blackwell load_in_4bit=True, # QLoRA NF4 full_finetuning=False,
)
model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=32, lora_alpha=32, # rank=alpha (Unsloth recommended) target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj", "gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj"], lora_dropout=0, bias="none", use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth", # +30% ctx, ~+1.9% time random_state=3407,
)
```
TrainingArguments: `per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, optim="paged_adamw_8bit", learning_rate=2e-4, bf16=True, logging_steps=1`. This mirrors NVIDIA's published 5090 benchmark (Llama-3.1-8B, rank 32 on all linear layers, bs=2/grad-accum=4 on the Alpaca set: ~2x faster, ~70% less VRAM than FlashAttention-2). For 32B set max_seq_length=2048 and per_device_batch=1 to stay under 32 GB.

extras.name: verl-wsl2-single-5090-grpo-lora-qwen-1.5b-to-7b
extras.note:
Single-5090 GRPO with a colocated vLLM rollout, inside WSL2 (veRL is Linux-first — Ray+vLLM+FSDP). On the WSL2 cu128 base: `pip install "verl[vllm]==0.8.0"` (pulls FSDP/vLLM extras; if it tries to install a non-cu128 torch, install torch==2.9.0+cu128 FIRST then `pip install verl==0.8.0 --no-deps` and add deps manually). Prep data: `python3 examples/data_preprocess/gsm8k.py --local_dir ~/data/gsm8k`. Single-GPU GRPO launch (adapted from the upstream 1-GPU example — keep tensor_model_parallel_size=1 and shrink batches for 32 GB):
```bash
python3 -m verl.trainer.main_ppo \ algorithm.adv_estimator=grpo \ data.train_files=$HOME/data/gsm8k/train.parquet \ data.val_files=$HOME/data/gsm8k/test.parquet \ data.train_batch_size=64 \ data.max_prompt_length=512 data.max_response_length=1024 \ actor_rollout_ref.model.path=Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct \ actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.lr=1e-6 \ actor_rollout_ref.actor.ppo_mini_batch_size=16 \ actor_rollout_ref.actor.use_kl_loss=True \ actor_rollout_ref.actor.fsdp_config.param_offload=True \ actor_rollout_ref.actor.fsdp_config.optimizer_offload=True \ actor_rollout_ref.model.enable_gradient_checkpointing=True \ actor_rollout_ref.model.lora_rank=32 actor_rollout_ref.model.lora_alpha=32 \ actor_rollout_ref.rollout.name=vllm \ actor_rollout_ref.rollout.tensor_model_parallel_size=1 \ actor_rollout_ref.rollout.gpu_memory_utilization=0.4 \ trainer.n_gpus_per_node=1 trainer.nnodes=1 trainer.total_epochs=2
```
Key 32 GB levers: gpu_memory_utilization=0.4 (rollout shares VRAM with FSDP shards — too high = OOM during generation), param_offload+optimizer_offload=True (push optimizer/params to the 64 GB system RAM), LoRA (lora_rank=32) instead of full-param to cut memory hard, train_batch_size=64 not 1024. 1.5B is comfortable; 7B is the cramped ceiling on one card. Scale-out: bump n_gpus_per_node and drop offload on rented multi-GPU.

extras.name: openrlhf-wsl2-ray-vllm-deepspeed-7b-grpo
extras.note:
OpenRLHF GRPO/PPO on a single 32 GB 5090 in WSL2 (README shows 7B full RLHF across multiple 24 GB 4090s, so 7B fits one 32 GB card with ZeRO-3 + offload). Cleanest path is the NGC container (already cu13-class, sm_120 works): `docker run --gpus all -it --shm-size=16g -v $HOME/openrlhf:/workspace nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.11-py3` then `pip install openrlhf[vllm]==0.10.3`. Bare-WSL2 alt: install on the cu128 torch base, `pip install openrlhf[vllm]==0.10.3 deepspeed ray`. Start a local Ray head: `ray start --head --num-gpus 1`. GRPO launch (colocate vLLM + actor on the one GPU; ZeRO-3 + paged optimizer + CPU offload):
```bash
python3 -m openrlhf.cli.train_ppo_ray \ --pretrain Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct \ --advantage_estimator group_norm \ --colocate_all_models \ --vllm_num_engines 1 --vllm_tensor_parallel_size 1 \ --vllm_gpu_memory_utilization 0.4 \ --zero_stage 3 --adam_offload --gradient_checkpointing \ --ref_reward_offload \ --micro_train_batch_size 1 --train_batch_size 64 \ --micro_rollout_batch_size 1 --rollout_batch_size 64 \ --n_samples_per_prompt 8 \ --prompt_max_len 512 --generate_max_len 1024 \ --actor_learning_rate 5e-7 --bf16 --flash_attn
```
32 GB survival kit: --colocate_all_models (single-GPU placement), --vllm_gpu_memory_utilization 0.4, --zero_stage 3 --adam_offload (optimizer state to the 64 GB RAM), --ref_reward_offload, micro batch=1. For LoRA-RL add `--lora_rank 32 --lora_alpha 32`. v0.10.2's Muon optimizer (--optimizer muon) can be tried for SFT/DPO. Use OpenRLHF over veRL when you prefer the explicit Ray actor/critic/reward role model; otherwise veRL is the more flexible default.

extras.name: trl-unsloth-dpo-preference-tuning-no-ray-cheapest-path
extras.note:
The CHEAPEST preference-tuning path on this rig — DPO/ORPO/KTO with NO Ray, NO vLLM, NO DeepSpeed, Windows-native via Unsloth + HF TRL. Best when you have a preference dataset (chosen/rejected) and want alignment without standing up an RL cluster. Install on the cu128 base: `pip install unsloth trl peft bitsandbytes`. Load a 14B in 4-bit (DPO holds a policy + an implicit/frozen reference; Unsloth's PatchDPOTrainer shares the base to fit both in 32 GB):
```python
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel, PatchDPOTrainer
PatchDPOTrainer() # call BEFORE importing DPOTrainer — halves memory by reusing the base as the ref
from trl import DPOTrainer, DPOConfig
model, tok = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( "unsloth/Qwen3-14B-bnb-4bit", max_seq_length=2048, load_in_4bit=True)
model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=32, lora_alpha=32, target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj","gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj"], use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth")
args = DPOConfig(per_device_train_batch_size=1, gradient_accumulation_steps=8, beta=0.1, learning_rate=5e-6, optim="paged_adamw_8bit", bf16=True, max_length=2048, max_prompt_length=1024, logging_steps=1)
trainer = DPOTrainer(model=model, ref_model=None, args=args, train_dataset=ds, processing_class=tok)
trainer.train()
```
Why ref_model=None: with Unsloth+PEFT the frozen base IS the reference (LoRA deltas disabled), so you do NOT pay for a second full model — that is what makes 14B DPO fit in 32 GB. Swap DPOTrainer->ORPOTrainer (no ref at all, beta becomes lambda) or KTOTrainer for unpaired feedback. This covers the studio's realistic 'align my style/instruction model' need without touching veRL/OpenRLHF.

extras.name: axolotl-wsl2-qlora-yaml-flash-attn-cu128
extras.note:
Axolotl for reproducible YAML-driven (Q)LoRA/full-SFT/DPO/ORPO with FSDP+DeepSpeed support — run in WSL2 (its bnb/flash-attn/deepspeed stack is Linux-first; the 5090 issue #2525 root cause was exactly the pre-2.7 torch, fixed by a cu128 torch). ```yaml
base_model: Qwen/Qwen3-14B
load_in_4bit: true
adapter: qlora
lora_r: 32
lora_alpha: 32
lora_dropout: 0.0
lora_target_linear: true
sequence_len: 4096
sample_packing: true
pad_to_sequence_len: true
flash_attention: true
micro_batch_size: 2
gradient_accumulation_steps: 4
optimizer: paged_adamw_8bit
learning_rate: 0.0002
bf16: auto

extras.name: llamacpp-blackwell-build-and-lora-export-merge
extras.note: llama.cpp on Blackwell — for SERVING your fine-tuned adapters as GGUF and for partial CPU/RAM offload of big MoE models the 64 GB RAM unlocks. CRITICAL Blackwell build gotcha (NVIDIA migration guide + community benchmarks): use CUDA Toolkit 12.8 EXACTLY (newer toolkits trigger MMQ/MXFP4 'mma with block scale not supported' PTX crashes on sm_120) and build with MMQ on, cuBLAS-force off. Windows-native build: `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS=OFF && cmake --build build --config Release -j`. Serve a 32B dense GGUF fully on-GPU: `build\bin\llama-server -m model-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0` (FA + q8_0 KV cache stretches 32 GB to long context). MoE partial offload using the 64 GB RAM (e.g. a large MoE that won't fully fit VRAM): `llama-server -m moe.gguf -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 24 -c 16384 -fa` — --n-cpu-moe keeps the dense/attention path on the 5090 and pushes N expert layers to CPU+RAM. To use a fine-tuned LoRA: either merge in Unsloth (`model.save_pretrained_gguf("out", tok, quantization_method="q4_k_m")`) for a single merged GGUF, or convert the base then run with `--lora adapter.gguf` for hot-swappable adapters. This is the bridge from 'I trained a LoRA' to 'it serves in my local studio loop.' If ggml custom kernels crash on a given model, cuBLAS is the stable fallback path.

extras.name: wsl2-blackwell-setup-the-linux-first-escalation-base
extras.note: One-time WSL2 foundation that every Linux-first engine here (veRL, OpenRLHF, Axolotl, LLaMA-Factory, vLLM) sits on — do this ONCE, reuse for all. Host (Win11, PowerShell admin): `wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04`; `wsl --update`; reboot. Confirm host NVIDIA driver R570+ (CUDA 12.8 requirement). Inside Ubuntu-24.04: do NOT install a Linux NVIDIA driver (WSL passes the Windows driver through /usr/lib/wsl/lib) — install only the CUDA 12.8 TOOLKIT if you compile (e.g. llama.cpp/flash-attn): `wget https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/wsl-ubuntu/x86_64/cuda-keyring_1.1-1_all.deb && sudo dpkg -i cuda-keyring_1.1-1_all.deb && sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y cuda-toolkit-12-8`. Docker-in-WSL with GPU: install Docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit, then `docker run --gpus all` mounts /usr/lib/wsl/lib automatically. Python env: `python3 -m venv ~/ml && source ~/ml/bin/activate && pip install torch==2.9.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 && pip install numpy==1.26.4`. Verify GPU is real (not CPU fallback): `python -c "import torch;print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0), torch.cuda.get_device_capability())"` must show 'NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090' and (12,0). Memory note: give WSL2 plenty of the 64 GB RAM for CPU-offload to work — create %UserProfile%\.wslconfig with `[wsl2]` + `memory=56GB` + `swap=32GB` so ZeRO/FSDP optimizer offload has room. INSTALL TORCH LAST in every venv; pin numpy<2.

research.domain: Diffusion inference engines & accelerators (image/video diffusion runtimes & accelerators — the engine layer, not the models)
research.notes: WAVE-2 SYNTHESIS — what the new engines change for the RTX 5090 / 32 GB rig: The single hard constraint on this lane is that the flagship 2026 image models no longer fit in 32 GB at native precision. FLUX.2-dev is ~32B params: BF16 ≈ 64 GB, and even FP8 ≈ 32 GB sits right at the VRAM ceiling (text encoders + VAE + activations push it over). So on this rig there is no "just load it" path for FLUX.2-dev — every workflow that wants the big model MUST quantize or offload. Wave 1 gave the ComfyUI-side tools (ComfyUI-GGUF, Nunchaku, TensorRT, the *Cache nodes). Wave 2 adds the THREE pieces that close the gap: (1) **torchao** is the upstream PyTorch mechanism — it is *why* NVFP4/MXFP8 exist in Diffusers/ComfyUI/xDiT on Blackwell at all; NVFP4 (1.5–1.7x faster, ~4-bit, hardware-accelerated on Blackwell's 5th-gen tensor cores) is the headline Blackwell win and lives in torchao's prototype.mx_formats. (2) **stable-diffusion.cpp** is the only engine here that treats the 64 GB system RAM as a first-class tier: `--offload-to-cpu` streams DiT weights from RAM to VRAM on demand, so FLUX.2-dev Q8 (~32 GB of weights) runs on a 32 GB card with the overflow living in RAM — the same llama.cpp-style RAM-offload trick this rig already relies on for LLMs, now for diffusion, with zero Python/Torch dependency hell. (3) **InvokeAI** is the Apache-2.0 escape hatch from ComfyUI's GPL — same FLUX.2/Qwen-Image/GGUF capability, production frontend, license-clean for a commercial studio. SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT CONFIG TAKEAWAY: **On Blackwell, the PyTorch CUDA build you install IS the ceiling.** Use the **cu130 nightly** (torch ≥ 2.12.dev), not cu128 — cu128 nightly *runs* on sm_120 but is missing the NVFP4 kernels, silently leaving Blackwell's best feature on the table. Then never let anything downgrade it: exclude `torch` from every custom-node `requirements.txt`, never `pip install xformers` (its PyPI wheels cap at sm_89 and silently reinstall stable torch). For the non-Torch path, build stable-diffusion.cpp with `-DSD_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120` against CUDA Toolkit ≥ 12.8. Decision tree for this rig: FLUX.2-dev quality → Nunchaku NVFP4 (fastest, ~3x) or sd.cpp Q8 + `--offload-to-cpu` (fits via RAM, no Torch); SDXL/SD3.5/FLUX.1 → ComfyUI + SageAttention(Blackwell wheel) + TensorRT/torchao; license-clean commercial frontend → InvokeAI; CLI/scriptable/CI → stable-diffusion.cpp.

engines.summary: The upstream PyTorch quantization library that makes NVFP4/MXFP8 real on Blackwell — it is the mechanism Diffusers, ComfyUI, and xDiT call under the hood. Exposes NVFP4DynamicActivationNVFP4WeightConfig and MXDynamicActivationMXWeightConfig (torchao.prototype.mx_formats.inference_workflow); applied via Diffusers' PipelineQuantizationConfig + TorchAoConfig, then torch.compile (compile_repeated_blocks(fullgraph=True)). NVFP4 is Blackwell's headline format — ~4-bit with hardware-accelerated 5th-gen-tensor-core matmul — cutting FLUX.1-dev/QwenImage memory ~60% while running 1.5–1.7x faster than BF16. Critical Blackwell gotcha: NVFP4 kernels ship only in the cu130 nightly (torch >=2.12.dev, torchao >=0.17.dev); the cu128 nightly executes on sm_120 but silently omits NVFP4. Not a standalone server — a library you compose into Diffusers/ComfyUI — but it is the single most important Blackwell-enablement primitive in this lane.
