Launch: `sd-cli.exe -m flux2-dev-Q8_0.gguf --vae flux2-ae.safetensors --clip_l clip_l.safetensors --t5xxl t5xxl_fp16.safetensors -p "..." --steps 28 --cfg-scale 4.0 -H 1024 -W 1024 --diffusion-fa --offload-to-cpu --vae-tiling -t -1`. `--offload-to-cpu` keeps weights in RAM and pages them into VRAM on demand (this is what makes a 32 GB weight set fit on a 32 GB card); `--diffusion-fa` enables flash attention; `--vae-tiling` keeps VAE decode under the VRAM cap. If still tight add `--clip-on-cpu` and/or `--vae-on-cpu`. For a smaller/faster footprint drop to Q4_K (`--type` already baked into the GGUF) — Q4 is the practical quality floor for FLUX. Slower than ComfyUI+NVFP4 but it RUNS where pure-VRAM engines OOM, with zero Python/Torch.

extras.name: torchao-nvfp4-flux-diffusers-cu130
extras.note: NVFP4 FLUX.1-dev in Diffusers on the 5090 — ~1.6x faster + ~60% less VRAM vs BF16. MUST use the cu130 nightly (cu128 runs but silently lacks NVFP4 kernels). Env (Python 3.11): `pip install --pre torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu130`; `pip install --pre torchao --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu130`; `pip install diffusers transformers accelerate sentencepiece protobuf`. Pinned versions that work: torch 2.12.0.dev20260315+cu130, torchao 0.17.0.dev20260316+cu130. Code: `from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline, TorchAoConfig, PipelineQuantizationConfig`; `import torch`; `from torchao.prototype.mx_formats.inference_workflow import NVFP4DynamicActivationNVFP4WeightConfig`; `cfg = NVFP4DynamicActivationNVFP4WeightConfig(use_dynamic_per_tensor_scale=True, use_triton_kernel=True)`; `pqc = PipelineQuantizationConfig(quant_mapping={"transformer": TorchAoConfig(cfg)})`; `pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, quantization_config=pqc).to("cuda")`; `pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(fullgraph=True)`. For batch_size=1 use `torch.compile(..., mode='reduce-overhead')` (CUDA graphs). NVFP4 needs CUDA capability >=10.0 (5090 = sm_120 qualifies). If NVFP4 LPIPS drift is too high for a model, swap the config for MXFP8: `from torchao.prototype.mx_formats.inference_workflow import MXDynamicActivationMXWeightConfig` + `from torchao.prototype.mx_formats import KernelPreference`; `MXDynamicActivationMXWeightConfig(activation_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, weight_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, kernel_preference=KernelPreference.AUTO)` (~1.26x, much lower LPIPS).

extras.name: comfyui-blackwell-win-clean-install-cu130
extras.note: ComfyUI on the 5090 (sm_120), Windows-native, no WSL2. Use Python 3.11 or 3.13 (match your SageAttention wheel). Install Blackwell-capable Torch FIRST: `pip install --pre torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu130`. Then `pip install triton-windows` (stock Triton is Linux-only; the Windows fork is needed for SageAttention/torch.compile). TWO non-negotiable rules: (1) NEVER `pip install xformers` — its PyPI wheels cap at sm_89 (Ada) and silently reinstall a STABLE torch, killing sm_120; (2) edit every custom-node `requirements.txt` to REMOVE the `torch`/`torchvision`/`torchaudio` lines before installing, or pip's resolver downgrades your nightly. Launch flags for the 32 GB card: `python main.py --use-pytorch-cross-attention --highvram --async-offload --pin-shared-memory`. Do NOT pass `--use-sage-attention` globally (black outputs on some models) — patch it per-workflow via the ComfyUI-KJNodes 'Patch Sage Attention' node instead.

extras.name: comfyui-gguf-flux2-dev-q8-5090
extras.note: FLUX.2-dev via city96 GGUF in ComfyUI on the 5090 (the wave-1 ComfyUI-GGUF path, pinned for this rig). Install node: `git clone https://github.com/city96/ComfyUI-GGUF custom_nodes/ComfyUI-GGUF` then `pip install gguf` into ComfyUI's venv (do NOT let its requirements pull torch). Download from huggingface `city96/FLUX.2-dev-gguf` — Q8_0 (~32 GB, near-lossless, sits at the VRAM ceiling so pair with --async-offload) or Q4_K_M (~16-18 GB, comfortable headroom, practical quality floor). Swap the standard checkpoint loader for `UnetLoaderGGUF` (DiT) + `DualCLIPLoaderGGUF` (quantized T5 text encoder to claw back VRAM) + standard VAE loader. Q8 ≈ near-identical to FP16; below Q4 hands/faces/text degrade. On Blackwell this combo gets ~2x the 4090's FLUX throughput thanks to native FP4 matmul. For the FLUX.2-Klein 9B variant, the same nodes work with the Klein GGUF and fit easily in 32 GB.

extras.name: nunchaku-nvfp4-flux-comfyui-5090-install
extras.note: Nunchaku NVFP4 (fastest FLUX path on the 5090, ~3.1x BF16). Clone the node: `git clone https://github.com/nunchaku-ai/ComfyUI-nunchaku custom_nodes/ComfyUI-nunchaku`. Install the engine wheel via the bundled `example_workflows/install_wheel.json` → NunchakuWheelInstaller node: set version=latest, torch_version=2.8 (or 2.9 to match your Blackwell torch), cuda_version=128, then Queue Prompt — it fetches `nunchaku-1.2.1+torch2.8-cp311-cp311-win_amd64.whl` from GitHub releases (manual equivalent: download that wheel and `python_embeded\python.exe -m pip install <wheel>`). On Blackwell pick the NVFP4 (svdq-fp4) model variants, NOT the INT4 ones — INT4 is the Ada/40-series path; NVFP4 is what the 5090's 5th-gen tensor cores accelerate.

extras.name: sageattention-blackwell-wheel-comfyui
extras.note: SageAttention 2.x on Blackwell (~35% faster diffusion sampling) — the wave-1 SageAttention engine, with the prebuilt sm_120 wheel for this rig. Prebuilt: `sageattention-2.2.0+cu128.torch2.11-cp311-cp311-win_amd64.whl` (built against torch 2.11.0.dev nightly, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.11). Install into ComfyUI's venv: `python_embeded\python.exe -m pip install sageattention-2.2.0+cu128.torch2.11-cp311-cp311-win_amd64.whl`. Avoid the global `--use-sage-attention` flag (can yield black outputs on some models). extras.name: comfyui-wan22-video-offload-32gb
extras.note: Video diffusion (Wan2.2 / LTX-2.3) on the 32 GB rig — two routes. ENGINE route (no Torch): stable-diffusion.cpp built per the sdcpp-blackwell-cuda-build recipe, run Wan with `sd-cli.exe -m wan2.2-*.gguf... --offload-to-cpu --vae-tiling --diffusion-fa` so frame tensors + weights spill to the 64 GB RAM (video VAE decode is the VRAM spike — `--vae-tiling` + `--vae-on-cpu` are essential). COMFYUI route: install the cu130-nightly clean env (comfyui-blackwell-win recipe), use GGUF Wan2.2 via UnetLoaderGGUF + `--async-offload --pin-shared-memory`, and keep latent frame count modest (e.g. 49–81 frames @ 480–720p) — going wider OOMs before the DiT does. LTX-2.3 is the lighter/faster of the two for iteration. For acceleration stack the wave-1 *Cache nodes (TeaCache/FBCache via Comfy-WaveSpeed) on top — they cut redundant steps and matter more on video than stills.

extras.name: diffusers-blackwell-quants-benchmark-harness
extras.note: Sayak Paul's reproducible NVFP4/MXFP8 benchmark + accuracy harness (benchmark.py, compute_lpips.py, run_drawbench_local.py). research.notes:
WAVE-2 SYNTHESIS — what the new engines change for this rig, and the one configuration takeaway. THE ONE LOAD-BEARING FACT (verified 2026-06-02): on Blackwell sm_120, the binary you install matters more than the engine you choose. As of June 2026 STABLE PyTorch wheels still compile only up to sm_90 (Hopper) — pytorch/pytorch#164342 is still OPEN — so on the RTX 5090 the *default* `pip install torch` either errors ("no kernel image is available for execution on the device") or silently falls back. The fix is the same for the entire torch ecosystem (PyTorch, vLLM, Unsloth, ComfyUI, diffusers, TRL): install the **cu128 (or cu130) nightly** index, OR the NVIDIA NGC `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.xx` container, OR build from source with `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0`. Every torch-based recipe below pins cu128-nightly for this reason. The single most important configuration takeaway for this lane: PIN THE WHEEL TO cu128/cu130-NIGHTLY AND PIN THE CUDA TOOLKIT TO 12.8 — newer toolkits (13.x) trigger MMQ/MXFP4 ptxas crashes on sm_120 in llama.cpp (issue #19662), and stable torch wheels miss sm_120 entirely. WHAT THE NEW ENGINES CHANGE:
1. KTransformers is the biggest unlock for the 64 GB-RAM half of this rig. It is the only engine here purpose-built to run a 671B-class MoE (DeepSeek-V3/V4, Kimi) on ONE 32 GB GPU by pinning attention + a hot expert on-GPU and streaming cold experts from system RAM — 20+ tok/s decode on a single 5090 (SOSP'25 paper). This is the "punch above 32 GB VRAM" path that llama.cpp's `--n-cpu-moe` approximates but KTransformers does with a real heterogeneous scheduler. For a local studio it means a frontier-class reasoning model is reachable on the box you already own.
2. tinygrad and MLC-LLM are cross-platform-reference + experimentation engines, not your production server. tinygrad (MIT, 0.13.0, UOp IR) is the cleanest place to *understand* a compiler and to target weird backends (Mesa NIR/NVK, WebGPU) — keep it as reference. MLC-LLM (Apache-2.0, TVM-backed) earns its slot as the ONLY engine here that compiles one model definition to CUDA *and* WebGPU/Vulkan/Metal — if the studio ever ships an in-browser demo (WebLLM) it is the path, but its cu128 support is nightly-wheel and JIT-compiled, so it lags llama.cpp/vLLM for day-to-day 5090 serving.
3. ROCm stays pure reference — there is no AMD GPU in this rig. Catalogued as the non-NVIDIA substrate so the KB is honest about portability: HIP SDK 7.1.1 is Windows-native but RDNA-only (gfx1100/1200), and stable ROCm 7.2.x is Linux-first for Instinct. Nothing to install here. LANE BOTTOM LINE FOR THIS RIG: for local LLM serving the production stack is llama.cpp (Windows-native, easiest) and vLLM (WSL2, fastest for batched/AWQ); for fine-tuning it is Unsloth-in-WSL2; for diffusion/ComfyUI it is cu128/cu130-nightly torch; for frontier-MoE-on-a-budget it is KTransformers. All five live or die by the nightly-wheel + CUDA-12.8 pin above.

engines.summary: MLC-LLM is a universal LLM deployment engine built on Apache TVM's Unity/Relax compiler (the same TVM wave-1 catalogued, specialized for LLMs). You convert HF weights to the MLC format (convert_weight → gen_config → compile), and TVM codegens an optimized library for the chosen --device: CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, ROCm, WebGPU, or WASM. MLCEngine exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST/Python/JS API across all of them. Apache-2.0. Its defining feature is reach: it is the engine behind WebLLM (in-browser, WebGPU) and the only one in this lane that compiles one model to both a 5090 and a browser tab. For THIS rig, Blackwell works through mlc-llm-nightly-cu128 wheels + JIT (no semver release; install `--pre` from mlc.ai/wheels). It is the right tool when cross-platform/in-browser is the requirement, but for plain local 5090 serving llama.cpp (easier on Windows) and vLLM (faster batched) win — hence 'situational'.

engines.summary: tinygrad is a pure-Python ML framework/compiler from George Hotz's tiny corp that has matured into a genuinely portable runtime. Its core abstraction is the UOp ('Unified Operation') IR — a single ~90-op IR that represents the tensor graph, the scheduled kernel graph, AND the linearized instructions, the only IR in the whole compiler. It lazily builds a graph and uses search to schedule kernels, then codegens to many backends: CUDA/PTX and the new open NVK/NAK path (via a Mesa NIR backend added in 0.12, Jan 2026), AMD HIP plus tiny corp's own 'AM' userspace driver (RDNA3/3.5/4, MI300X), Apple Metal, Qualcomm, WebGPU, OpenCL, CPU/LLVM, and x86 assembly. MIT-licensed; 0.13.0 shipped 2026-05-22. For THIS rig it is situational: the CUDA backend reaches sm_120, and it's the cleanest codebase in this lane to *learn* compiler internals or prototype a custom backend — but for production training/inference on the 5090, PyTorch+cuDNN and llama.cpp/vLLM are faster and better-supported. Keep it as the 'understand the compiler / weird-backend' tool.

extras.name: pytorch-blackwell-cu128-nightly-base (sm_120 foundation for the WHOLE torch lane)
extras.note:
THE prerequisite for every torch engine on this rig. As of 2026-06-02 STABLE torch wheels compile only up to sm_90 — on a 5090 the default install errors 'no kernel image is available for execution on the device'. Three working paths, pick one:
(A) NIGHTLY cu128 (simplest, native Windows OK): python -m pip install --pre torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu128 Verify: python -c "import torch;print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.get_device_capability())" -> expect (12,0)
(B) cu130 NIGHTLY (preferred for diffusion / NVFP4 paths — ComfyUI blog says cu128 misses some Blackwell FP4 kernels): python -m pip install --pre torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu130
(C) NVIDIA NGC container (most reproducible, WSL2/Docker): docker run --gpus all -it nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.05-py3 (ships torch built for sm_120).
If building from source: set TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST="12.0" before python setup.py develop, with CUDA Toolkit 12.8. PIN CUDA TOOLKIT TO 12.8 — 13.x triggers sm_120 ptxas/MMQ failures across this ecosystem. Caveat: do NOT let xformers pull a stable torch back over your nightly (it silently downgrades cu130->cu128); pin xformers to a matching nightly or drop it for SDPA+Triton.

extras.name: llamacpp-blackwell-build-and-serve (Windows-native, CUDA 12.8, NVFP4 MMQ)
extras.note:
Easiest production LLM server on this rig — builds native on Windows, no WSL2. Use CUDA Toolkit 12.8 (NOT 13.x — 13.x crashes sm_120 MMQ/MXFP4 kernels, issue #19662). Build (PowerShell, VS2022 + CUDA 12.8 installed): cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON cmake --build build --config Release -j
Use build b8967 (2026-04-29) or later for native NVFP4 MMQ tensor-core acceleration on sm_120. Serve a dense 32B Q4_K_M fully on the 5090 (fits 32 GB):.\build\bin\Release\llama-server -m model-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
For a big MoE (e.g. a 100B+ MoE that won't fit) keep its expert layers on CPU/RAM (64 GB headroom): llama-server -m moe.gguf -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 24 -c 32768 -fa --cache-type-k q8_0 (--n-cpu-moe N puts the first N layers' MoE weights in system RAM; raise N until VRAM fits, lower for speed; --cpu-moe = all experts on CPU.) -fa (flash-attn) + q8_0 KV cache roughly halves KV memory vs f16 with negligible quality loss; on a 5090 a 32B Q4_K_M runs comfortably >40 tok/s.

extras.name: vllm-wsl2-5090-awq-serve (fastest batched serving, ~140 tok/s Qwen3-14B-AWQ)
extras.note:
vLLM has no native Windows build — run it in WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04). Verified working stack: torch 2.9.0+cu128, vLLM 0.17.1, CUDA 12.8, NVIDIA driver 581.80+, WSL2 2.7.0. Setup: wsl --update (host PowerShell, get WSL2 >= 2.7.0 so CUDA-graph capture works) # in Ubuntu: python -m venv vllm && source vllm/bin/activate pip install --pre torch==2.9.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 pip install vllm==0.17.1
Serve a 14B AWQ (4-bit) on the 5090: python3 -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model /models/Qwen3-14B-AWQ --quantization awq_marlin --dtype float16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --attention-backend flashinfer --swap-space 4 --port 11436 --served-model-name qwen3-14b
DO NOT pass --enforce-eager (CUDA graphs now work on WSL2 2.7.0). Benchmark on this exact setup: ~140 tok/s with CUDA graphs vs ~17 tok/s with --enforce-eager (8x) and ~111 tok/s Ollama q4_K_M. WSL2 gotchas that block the GPU: set [wsl2] memory=56GB in C:\Users\<you>\.wslconfig; remove Tailscale inside WSL; mask nvidia-cdi-refresh. For a 32B AWQ drop --max-model-len to ~4096 and keep --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90.

extras.name: unsloth-qlora-14b-wsl2 (fine-tune a 14B in 32 GB VRAM, paged_adamw_8bit)
extras.note:
Unsloth officially supports Blackwell RTX 50-series (5060-5090). Windows-native is painful (sm_120 kernel gaps); run in WSL2 Ubuntu. Install on the cu128-nightly base (see pytorch recipe): pip install --pre torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu128 pip install unsloth unsloth_zoo bitsandbytes # for kernel gaps, Unsloth Studio's curl installer gives a Blackwell-tuned py3.13 venv
QLoRA config that fits a 14B in 32 GB VRAM (verified shape: bs2 x grad-accum4, rank32, all linear layers): from unsloth import FastLanguageModel model, tok = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(model_name='unsloth/Qwen2.5-14B-bnb-4bit', max_seq_length=2048, load_in_4bit=True, dtype=None) model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=32, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0, bias='none', target_modules=['q_proj','k_proj','v_proj','o_proj','gate_proj','up_proj','down_proj'], use_gradient_checkpointing='unsloth', random_state=3407) from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig trainer = SFTTrainer(model=model, tokenizer=tok, train_dataset=ds, args=SFTConfig(per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, warmup_steps=5, learning_rate=2e-4, fp16=False, bf16=True, logging_steps=1, optim='paged_adamw_8bit', weight_decay=0.01, lr_scheduler_type='linear', max_seq_length=2048, output_dir='out')) trainer.train()
paged_adamw_8bit (bitsandbytes paged optimizer) pages optimizer state to the 64 GB system RAM on OOM spikes — load-bearing for fitting 14B+gradients in 32 GB. use_gradient_checkpointing='unsloth' is the memory-cheapest mode. Unsloth's own benchmark: ~70% less VRAM, single Blackwell GPU fine-tunes up to ~40B.

extras.name: ktransformers-deepseek-moe-offload (671B-class MoE on ONE 5090 + 64 GB RAM)
extras.note:
The 'punch above 32 GB VRAM' path — run a frontier MoE locally. Best in WSL2 Ubuntu (also Windows-native since Aug 2024). Stack: CUDA 12.8, torch cu128-nightly, AVX-512/AMX CPU (the Ultra 9 qualifies). Install: pip install --pre torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu128 pip install ktransformers # or build from source for newest MoE kernels (USE_BALANCE_SERVE=1 for the v0.2+ server)
Run a quantized DeepSeek-V3/V4 (attention+hot-expert on GPU, cold experts streamed from the 64 GB RAM): python -m ktransformers.local_chat --model_path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3 --gguf_path /models/DeepSeek-V3-Q4_K_M --cpu_infer 16 --max_new_tokens 1024 --optimize_config_path ktransformers/optimize/optimize_rules/DeepSeek-V3-Chat.yaml
or the OpenAI-compatible server: python ktransformers/server/main.py --model_path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3 --gguf_path /models/DeepSeek-V3-Q4_K_M --cpu_infer 16 --port 10002
--cpu_infer = CPU threads for expert compute (set near physical core count). The optimize_rules YAML is the placement policy (which tensors GPU vs CPU) — pick the one matching your model. Result on this rig class: 20+ tok/s decode for DeepSeek-V4-Flash on a SINGLE RTX 5090; ~2-5x slower than fully-on-GPU but runs a model that otherwise needs 400+ GB VRAM. 64 GB RAM is the realistic floor for a heavily-quantized V3/V4; bigger MoE wants more RAM.

extras.name: comfyui-blackwell-cu130-portable (SDXL/Flux diffusion on the 5090, FP8 tensor cores)
extras.note:
Diffusion is a core studio workload. ComfyUI has day-1 Blackwell support; on Windows use the portable build (no WSL2/Docker). Easiest: download ComfyUI_windows_portable, run update\update_comfyui_and_python_dependencies.bat to pull a cu128/cu130 build, then run_nvidia_gpu.bat. Manual venv path: python -m pip install --pre torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu130 pip install -r requirements.txt python main.py --use-pytorch-cross-attention # avoid xformers (it can force-downgrade cu130->cu128)
Why cu130 over cu128 for diffusion: ComfyUI's official blog notes cu128 nightly misses some Blackwell NVFP4 kernels and can run slower; cu130-nightly enables the 5th-gen FP8/NVFP4 tensor-core path. On a 5090, FP8 native tensor-core support cuts VRAM ~40% and speeds generation vs BF16 — load Flux/SDXL in FP8 where the workflow supports it. For Triton/SageAttention/FlashAttention on Windows Blackwell (faster Flux), follow Comfy-Org discussion #6980 (prebuilt Blackwell wheels for triton-windows + sageattention). 32 GB VRAM comfortably runs Flux.1-dev FP8 + SDXL refiner in one workflow.

extras.name: tensorrt-llm-vs-trt-for-rtx-decision (when to pay the build cost on this rig)
extras.note: Wave-1 catalogued TensorRT-for-RTX; this is the OPERATIONAL decision rule for THIS rig so you don't over-invest. Use NGC containers to dodge the sm_120 wheel problem entirely: docker run --gpus all -it nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.05-py3 (ships torch+TensorRT built for sm_120, CUDA 12.8). DECISION: (1) For LLM serving, do NOT reach for TensorRT-LLM first — engine builds are slow and brittle on a single consumer GPU; llama.cpp (Windows-native) and vLLM (WSL2) get you 90% of the throughput with minutes-not-hours setup. (2) Use TensorRT only for FIXED-shape, latency-critical, repeatedly-run graphs: SDXL/Flux UNet via the ComfyUI TensorRT node, or an ONNX vision/audio model in a production loop — there the one-time engine build amortizes. (3) Always build the TRT engine on the SAME 5090 it will run on (engines are arch+driver-specific; sm_120 engines are not portable from sm_90 boxes). (4) Pin CUDA 12.8 and the matching TensorRT release; mismatched CUDA minor versions are the #1 cause of 'engine build succeeds, inference returns garbage' on Blackwell.

extras.name: GGUF quant picker for 32 GB VRAM
extras.note: Quant-vs-VRAM rule of thumb for a 32 GB 5090: dense models up to ~32B fit in Q4_K_M fully on-GPU (-ngl 99); a 70B needs Q4_K_M + partial CPU offload or a smaller quant. On Blackwell, NVFP4 (Nvidia block-scaled FP4) now has native MMQ tensor-core kernels in llama.cpp (build b8967+, 2026-04-29) — ~4 bits/weight, half the footprint of Q8 and ~25% smaller than Q4_K_M after metadata, with tensor-core speed. MXFP4 (OCP open standard) is mainly in ik_llama.cpp. Prefer NVFP4 GGUFs on this rig when available; fall back to Q4_K_M for broad compatibility.

extras.name: Blackwell sm_120 troubleshooting cheat-sheet (the 4 errors you WILL hit)
extras.note: Greppable failure->fix map for this rig: (1) 'CUDA error: no kernel image is available for execution on the device' -> you installed STABLE torch (sm_90 max); reinstall cu128/cu130 NIGHTLY or use NGC container. (2) llama.cpp ptxas 'Instruction mma with block scale not supported' or MMQ crash -> CUDA Toolkit is 13.x; downgrade to 12.8 OR build with -DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_MMQ=OFF. (3) vLLM ~17 tok/s (8x too slow) -> you passed --enforce-eager; remove it and ensure WSL2 >= 2.7.0 for CUDA-graph capture. (4) ComfyUI/Unsloth silently on stable torch after working -> xformers pulled a stable wheel over your nightly; pin xformers to a matching nightly or drop it for SDPA. Universal verify: python -c "import torch;print(torch.cuda.get_device_capability())" must print (12, 0).

proposed_additions.name: Triton (OpenAI Triton / triton-lang)
proposed_additions.why: The de-facto kernel authoring language for GPU-accelerated ML in 2026, used as a compilation target by KTransformers, vLLM, xFormers, and many others in this lane. Triton 3.x ships with native sm_120 (Blackwell) support and is the primary path for custom CUDA-equivalent kernels without writing raw CUDA C. It is a distinct runtime/compiler primitive that belongs in Foundational runtimes & compilers and is not currently represented.

proposed_additions.name: GGML / llama.cpp (core C/CUDA/Metal tensor library)
proposed_additions.why: GGML is the lowest-level tensor substrate underlying llama.cpp, whisper.cpp, and the entire GGUF ecosystem. It is a foundational runtime — not just a serving engine — with its own CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, and CPU SIMD backends. llama.cpp ships Blackwell-ready CUDA 12.8 builds and is the most widely deployed inference primitive for quantized models in 2026. Its absence from a Foundational runtimes & compilers lane is a significant gap.

proposed_additions.name: Apache TVM (Tensor Virtual Machine)
proposed_additions.why: TVM is the compilation backbone behind MLC-LLM (already in the wave) and a standalone foundational compiler in its own right, targeting CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, OpenCL, and WebGPU. As of v0.16+ it supports Blackwell via CUDA 12.8 codegen. Its role as the IR and optimization pass infrastructure for the entire MLC ecosystem makes it a distinct entry: MLC-LLM is the serving layer; TVM is the compiler primitive. Omitting TVM while including MLC-LLM creates an incomplete picture of the compilation stack.
